### Windows Terminal version

_No response_

### Windows build number

_No response_

### Other Software

When the shell outputs large amounts of text rapidly (such as streaming responses from AI tools or continuous build logs in a bash shell), the **WMI Provider Host (`WmiPrvSE.exe`)** spikes in CPU usage (consuming roughly 10% or more).

As soon as the text output stops, CPU usage immediately drops back to normal. This behavior is consistently reproducible inside `openconsole.exe` / Windows Terminal on Windows 10/11.



### Steps to reproduce

1. Open Windows Terminal (`openconsole.exe`).
2. Run a command or tool that streams a large volume of text very quickly (e.g., an AI chat CLI, heavy compilation logs, or `cat` on a massive file).
3. Open **Task Manager** and observe the CPU usage of **WMI Provider Host (`WmiPrvSE.exe`)**.

### Expected Behavior

Console rendering should handle high-speed text streams efficiently without triggering heavy WMI/performance counter queries or causing spikes in background system services like `WmiPrvSE.exe`.

### Actual Behavior

`WmiPrvSE.exe` spikes and hovers around 10% CPU usage while text is actively streaming into the console.

### Windows Terminal version

1.24.12741.0

### Windows build number

10.0.19045.6466

### Other Software

PowerShell 7.6.6 (.NET 10.0.12) with PSReadLine 2.4.5
RealVNC Server 5.2.3 (r8648), through which the keyboard input arrives

### Steps to reproduce

1. A machine whose only keyboard layout is English (United States).
2. Work on it through a VNC viewer whose own keyboard layout is Russian (RealVNC Server 5.2.3 runs on the machine).
3. In a PowerShell tab, type any Cyrillic letter, for example `п`.

### Expected Behavior

The letter appears at the prompt.

### Actual Behavior

The first Cyrillic letter ends PowerShell:

```
An error has occurred that was not properly handled. Additional information is shown below. The PowerShell process will exit.
Unhandled exception. System.ArgumentOutOfRangeException: Console key values must be between 0 and 255 inclusive. (Parameter 'key')
   at System.ConsoleKeyInfo..ctor(Char keyChar, ConsoleKey key, Boolean shift, Boolean alt, Boolean control)
   at System.ConsolePal.ReadKey(Boolean intercept)
   at Microsoft.PowerShell.Internal.VirtualTerminal.<>c.<ReadKey>b__40_0()
   at Microsoft.PowerShell.Internal.VirtualTerminal._TryIgnoreIOE[T](Func`1 f)
   at Microsoft.PowerShell.Internal.VirtualTerminal.ReadKey()
   at Microsoft.PowerShell.PSConsoleReadLine.ReadOneOrMoreKeys()
   at Microsoft.PowerShell.PSConsoleReadLine.ReadKeyThreadProc()

[process exited with code 3762504530 (0xe0434352)]
```

#### Where the key code comes from

https://github.com/microsoft/terminal/blob/7ff11ee107c984e236960ec948b450ccbc10187b/src/cascadia/TerminalCore/Terminal.cpp#L875-L879

`VkKeyScanW` returns a `SHORT`: -1 when the active layout has no key for the character, otherwise the virtual key in the low byte and the shift state in the high byte. `LOWORD` makes that an unsigned `WORD`, so `vkey == -1` is never true and the function returns 65535 where its comment promises 0. For a character that needs Shift it returns the shift state as well (`G` on the US layout: 0x147).

`Terminal::SendCharEvent` falls back to this function when a character event has neither a stored key-down nor a scan code (lines 733 to 741 of the same file). The value then leaves unchanged in the win32-input-mode sequence, `CSI 65535;0;1087;1;0;1_` for `п`, ends up in `KEY_EVENT_RECORD.wVirtualKeyCode`, and the constructor of .NET's `ConsoleKeyInfo` throws for anything above 255. `SendKeyEvent` already drops `vkey >= 0xff` (line 648), so this is the path that is left.

The function reads the same in v1.25.2733.0, in v1.26.2734.0 and on `main` (e90f9a5).

#### What I checked on the machine

- With only the US layout, `VkKeyScanW(L'п')` returns -1, which `LOWORD` makes 65535.
- A key event written with `WriteConsoleInputW` and read with `[Console]::ReadKey()` in pwsh 7.6.6 throws exactly this exception when `wVirtualKeyCode` is 65535 or 327, and returns `п` when it is 0 or `VK_PACKET`.
- Not traced: which events RealVNC injects for such a letter, that is, why no key-down is stored for it.

#### Suggested fix

```cpp
WORD Terminal::_VirtualKeyFromCharacter(const wchar_t ch) noexcept
{
    const auto vkey = VkKeyScanW(ch);
    return vkey == -1 ? 0 : LOBYTE(vkey);
}
```

Setting `"compatibility.input.forceVT": true` on the profile should avoid the crash, because the character then travels as text and conhost's `CharToKeyEvents` gives it virtual key 0. I have not confirmed that yet.

PowerShell/PowerShell#16090 (2021) shows the same exception, in Windows Terminal only, for a character injected by Clavier+. It was closed as external, and I found no issue for it in this repository.

### Windows Terminal version

1.24.12741.0

### Windows build number

10.0.26200.8894

### Other Software

System locale: Chinese (ANSI code page 936). "Beta: Use Unicode UTF-8 for worldwide language support" is **off**. (The cause below does not appear to depend on the code page, but I have only tested this configuration.)

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run in PowerShell 7 inside Windows Terminal:

   ```powershell
   $root = Join-Path ([IO.Path]::GetTempPath()) 'wt-link-repro'
   $ascii = Join-Path $root 'ascii'; $cjk = Join-Path $root '中文'
   New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force $ascii, $cjk | Out-Null
   Set-Content -LiteralPath "$ascii\a.txt" 'ascii'
   Set-Content -LiteralPath "$cjk\b.txt" 'cjk'
   function Get-FileUri([string]$p) {
     'file:///' + ((($p -replace '\\','/') -split '/' | % { [Uri]::EscapeDataString($_) -replace '%3A',':' }) -join '/')
   }
   $u1 = Get-FileUri "$ascii\a.txt"; $u2 = Get-FileUri "$cjk\b.txt"
   "`e]8;;$u1`aA) ASCII path`e]8;;`a"
   "`e]8;;$u2`aB) CJK path`e]8;;`a"
   $u1; $u2
   ```

   This prints two OSC 8 hyperlinks plus the raw URIs, e.g.
   `file:///C:/Users/<user>/AppData/Local/Temp/wt-link-repro/%E4%B8%AD%E6%96%87/b.txt`

2. Ctrl+click link **A**, then link **B**.
3. Ctrl+click the two raw URIs (detected by Terminal's URL detection).

### Expected Behavior

Both files open in the default app (Notepad), since both URIs are valid RFC 8089 file URIs with UTF-8 percent-encoding.

### Actual Behavior

- A (ASCII path): opens in Notepad.
- B (path containing `中文`, percent-encoded as UTF-8): nothing happens. No process is started and no error dialog is shown.
- Same result for the raw URIs: the ASCII one opens, the CJK one does nothing.

`_OpenHyperlinkHandler` (src/cascadia/TerminalApp/TerminalPage.cpp) passes the URI string unchanged to `ShellExecuteW`. Calling the same thing outside Terminal also fails:

```powershell
Start-Process 'file:///C:/.../wt-link-repro/%E4%B8%AD%E6%96%87/b.txt'
# -> The system cannot find the file specified.
```

The plain path `C:\...\wt-link-repro\中文\b.txt` opens fine, and so does the unescaped URI `file:///C:/.../wt-link-repro/中文/b.txt`.

The shell turns each `%xx` into a single character (byte value = code point, Latin-1 style) instead of decoding the bytes as UTF-8. I confirmed this by creating directories named after the possible mis-decodings:

| URI segment | File actually opened |
|---|---|
| `%E4%B8%AD%E6%96%87` (UTF-8 of `中文`) | directory `ä¸­æ–‡` (U+00E4 U+00B8 U+00AD U+00E6 U+0096 U+0087) |
| `%D6%D0%CE%C4` (GBK of `中文`) | directory `ÖÐÎÄ` (U+00D6 U+00D0 U+00CE U+00C4) |
| `中文` (not escaped) | directory `中文` (correct) |

Tools that emit OSC 8 links use UTF-8 percent-encoding as RFC 3986/8089 require, so any link to a path with non-ASCII characters opens the wrong path or silently fails.

A possible fix: for local `file:` URIs, unescape the path as UTF-8 (e.g. `Uri::UnescapeComponent`) and pass a local Windows path to `ShellExecuteW` instead of the raw URI.

Possibly related: #14116 (other `file://` URI forms that are not handled).

**Edit:** corrected the root-cause analysis. The first version said the shell decodes `%xx` with the ANSI code page; further testing (table above) showed it decodes each `%xx` as a separate character regardless of encoding.

---
*Disclosure: I used an AI assistant to help investigate and draft this report. I reproduced all steps and results above myself.*

   ```powershell
   "`e]8;;$u2`aB) CJK path`e]8;;`a"
   $u1; $u2
   ```

   This prints two OSC 8 hyperlinks plus the raw URIs, e.g.
   `file:///C:/Users/<user>/AppData/Local/Temp/wt-link-repro/%E4%B8%AD%E6%96%87/b.txt`

2. Ctrl+click link **A**, then link **B**.
3. Ctrl+click the two raw URIs (detected by Terminal's URL detection).

### Expected Behavior

Both files open in the default app (Notepad), since both URIs are valid RFC 8089 file URIs with UTF-8 percent-encoding.

### Actual Behavior

- A (ASCII path): opens in Notepad.
- B (path containing `中文`, percent-encoded as UTF-8): nothing happens. No process is started and no error dialog is shown.
- Same result for the raw URIs: the ASCII one opens, the CJK one does nothing.

`_OpenHyperlinkHandler` (src/cascadia/TerminalApp/TerminalPage.cpp) passes the URI string unchanged to `ShellExecuteW`. Calling the same thing outside Terminal also fails:

```powershell
Start-Process 'file:///C:/.../wt-link-repro/%E4%B8%AD%E6%96%87/b.txt'
# -> The system cannot find the file specified.
```

The plain path `C:\...\wt-link-repro\中文\b.txt` opens fine, and so does the unescaped URI `file:///C:/.../wt-link-repro/中文/b.txt`.

The shell turns each `%xx` into a single character (byte value = code point, Latin-1 style) instead of decoding the bytes as UTF-8. I confirmed this by creating directories named after the possible mis-decodings:

| URI segment | File actually opened |
|---|---|
| `%E4%B8%AD%E6%96%87` (UTF-8 of `中文`) | directory `ä¸­æ–‡` (U+00E4 U+00B8 U+00AD U+00E6 U+0096 U+0087) |
| `%D6%D0%CE%C4` (GBK of `中文`) | directory `ÖÐÎÄ` (U+00D6 U+00D0 U+00CE U+00C4) |
| `中文` (not escaped) | directory `中文` (correct) |

Tools that emit OSC 8 links use UTF-8 percent-encoding as RFC 3986/8089 require, so any link to a path with non-ASCII characters opens the wrong path or silently fails.

A possible fix: for local `file:` URIs, unescape the path as UTF-8 (e.g. `Uri::UnescapeComponent`) and pass a local Windows path to `ShellExecuteW` instead of the raw URI.

Possibly related: #14116 (other `file://` URI forms that are not handled).

**Edit:** corrected the root-cause analysis. The first version said the shell decodes `%xx` with the ANSI code page; further testing (table above) showed it decodes each `%xx` as a separate character regardless of encoding.

### Description of the new feature

I have a fine motor control issue, and the current scroll bar implementation in Terminal makes it hard for me to select and move the scroll bar.

I would like two things:

1. Increase the width so it makes it easier for me to target and manipulate the scroll bar.
2. Keep it always visible so I don't have to add targeting to the part of the window that brings up the scroll bar.

Another ticket like this was closed.  #18937. I understand the rationale that the developer didn't want to have different-sized scroll bars for different applications, which is why I think this should be a system-wide setting. This request is an accessibility need, and I apologize for my attitude, but accessibility needs should come first when designing app features. Design choices shouldn't make people's hands hurt.

body_text:
### Windows Terminal version

1.24.12741.0

### Windows build number

10.0.26200

### Other Software

WSL2 Ubuntu; found through Claude Code, which re-sends `ESC[?1049h` on view switches (anthropics/claude-code#80123). Related but different: #4389 is about console-API alternate buffers, while this is the VT alternate screen

### Steps to reproduce

Run `wt.exe -w new --size 100,30 wsl.exe -e bash repro.sh`, maximize the window after the first ruler, then press Enter twice:

```bash
# repro.sh
ruler() { for i in $(seq 1 16); do printf '%9d|' $((i*10)); done; echo; }
printf '\e[?1049h\e[2J\e[H'; stty size; ruler; read
printf '\e[?1049h\e[2J\e[H'; stty size; ruler; read
printf '\e[?1049l\e[?1049h\e[2J\e[H'; stty size; ruler; read
printf '\e[?1049l'
```

### Expected Behavior

The second and third rulers each print on one line, matching the width `stty size` reports

### Actual Behavior

The second ruler wraps at column 100, the launch width, while `stty size` reports the maximized size; the third ruler, sent after `?1049l`, prints at full width.

On `main`, `Terminal::UserResize` defers the main buffer's resize to `UseMainScreenBuffer` while the alternate screen is active, and `UseAlternateScreenBuffer` has no check for already being on the alternate screen, so it builds the new buffer from `_mutableViewport.Dimensions()`, which still holds the old size.

1.24.12741.0

### Windows build number

### Other Software

WSL2 Ubuntu; found through Claude Code, which re-sends `ESC[?1049h` on view switches (anthropics/claude-code#80123). Related but different: #4389 is about console-API alternate buffers, while this is the VT alternate screen

### Steps to reproduce

Run `wt.exe -w new --size 100,30 wsl.exe -e bash repro.sh`, maximize the window after the first ruler, then press Enter twice:

```bash
# repro.sh
ruler() { for i in $(seq 1 16); do printf '%9d|' $((i*10)); done; echo; }
printf '\e[?1049h\e[2J\e[H'; stty size; ruler; read
printf '\e[?1049h\e[2J\e[H'; stty size; ruler; read
printf '\e[?1049l\e[?1049h\e[2J\e[H'; stty size; ruler; read
printf '\e[?1049l'
```

### Expected Behavior

The second and third rulers each print on one line, matching the width `stty size` reports

### Actual Behavior

The second ruler wraps at column 100, the launch width, while `stty size` reports the maximized size; the third ruler, sent after `?1049l`, prints at full width.

On `main`, `Terminal::UserResize` defers the main buffer's resize to `UseMainScreenBuffer` while the alternate screen is active, and `UseAlternateScreenBuffer` has no check for already being on the alternate screen, so it builds the new buffer from `_mutableViewport.Dimensions()`, which still holds the old size.

body_text:
### Windows Terminal version

1.24.12741.0 & 1.26.2734.0 (Preview)

### Windows build number

10.0.26200.0

### Other Software

Custom profile file `Test-Profile.json`:
```json
{
    "$help": "https://aka.ms/terminal-documentation",
    "$schema": "https://aka.ms/terminal-profiles-schema",
    "profiles": {
        "list": [
            {
                "background": "#6A0000",
                "colorScheme": "One Half Dark",
                "commandline": "\"C:\\Program Files\\PowerShell\\7\\pwsh.exe\"",
                "elevate": true,
                "guid": "{4780855a-fa33-5cfd-ac42-4b65ea50bcab}",
                "hidden": false,
                "icon": "\ud83d\udca3",
                "name": "Test-Profile",
                "tabTitle": "Test-Profile"
            }
        ]
    }
```

### Steps to reproduce

1. Add new Extension that contains a Profile
   1. Create new Extension folder in Fragments directory: `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path "$($ENV:LOCALAPPDATA)\Microsoft\Windows Terminal\Fragments\Test-Profile\"` )
   2. Copy Profile's JSON file to Extension's folder: `Copy-Item -Path $SourceFile -Destination "$($ENV:LOCALAPPDATA)\Microsoft\Windows Terminal\Fragments\Test-Profile\Test-Profile.json"`
3. Start Windows Terminal
   - Confirm that new Profile now shows in Settings under _Profiles_
4. Disable newly created extension 
   1. _Settings_ > _Extensions_ > _Active Extensions_ > "Test-Profile": Toggle **Off**
5. _Save_
   - Profile should now be "Orphaned" as established in https://github.com/microsoft/terminal/pull/18188
6. Delete orphaned Profile in settings
   1. Select the orphaned Profile from: _Settings_ > _Profiles_ > _"Test Profile"_
   2. Delete Profile that is "No longer detected":  _Delete profile_
      - This causes the associated Profile in `settings.json` to be deleted
7. _Save_
8.  Re-Enable Extension
   1. _Settings_ > _Extensions_ > _Active Extensions_ > "Test-Profile": Toggle **On**
     - On Windows Terminal (1.24.12741.0): The Profile will (re)appear under _Added Profiles_ at the bottom of the _Extensions_ page in most circumstances [^1]
     - On Windows Terminal Preview (1.26.2734.0): The Profile will (re)appear under _Added Profiles_ at the bottom of the _Extensions_ page in some circumstances [^2]
9. **Profile will not reappear**
10. To "fix":
   1. Disable Profile's Extension (as described in Step 2 above) [^3]
   2. Close Windows Terminal
   3. Edit `state.json`, remove the Profile's GUID from `.generatedProfiles`
   4. Re-launch Windows Terminal
   5. Re-enable Extension (as described in Step 8 above) [^1]

[^1]: There are a few situations where it won't reappear, like after step 10.5, until after the Settings tab is closed and re-opened

[^2]: If reproduced exactly as shown, the profile will reappear. However, there are some additional bug(s) that seem to exist in the Preview build around (re-)enabling extensions after Windows Terminal Preview has been re-launched. I am not considering these directly related because it's a Preview build.
  That being said, so far, I have found:
    1: Add a new extension in a disabled state (via `disabledProfileSources`), launching Windows Terminal Preview, then enabling the extension causes the profile to not appear under _Added Profiles_ until after the Settings tab is re-opened.
    2: If Windows Terminal Preview is re-launched at step 7 above, re-enabling the Extension will cause the profile to never reappear under _Added Profiles_; It will appear at this point on the Production v1.24.* version even if it never gets added to `settings.json` which is very helpful in knowing that the profile is actually able to be processed and isn't corrupted.

[^3]: In my clean-room testing, I have encountered a situation where leaving it enabled caused the Profile to not be re-created until the Extension is disabled, WT is relaunched, and then enabled again but I wasn't able to determine the exact steps again.

### Expected Behavior

Profile should be re-created in `settings.json` under `.profiles.list` when re-enabling the Extension, which would cause the Profile to reappear under the Profiles list and as a selectable Profile in the New Tab Menu.
Potentially the Profile's GUID should also be removed from `state.json` when the profile is deleted?

### Actual Behavior

Profile is never re-created in `settings.json` and does not reappear under profiles or in the New Tab Menu.
Profile **does** reappear in _Settings_ > _New Tab Menu_ > _Add Entry_ > _Profile_. Selecting this does create the entry in `settings.json` under `.newTabMenu` but this won't be displayed.

### 🔎 Search Terms

generic function assignability, union return type, tuple union, TS2322, regression v4.2, generic type alias

### 🕗 Version & Regression Information

- This changed in commit [34f0e32 Bump version to 4.2.3 and LKG](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/commit/34f0e32dc667eb8c7b52b3fc4067316b4ae97774)
- This also reproduces on Nightly version

### ⏯ Playground Link

https://www.typescriptlang.org/play/?#-JwHMondb9HSXfSAx7PaivD5fJ78f7sbHA4o8MEEyFE6wwkRwhyIpQjTzePyBEKqCLqVHRWLxRLJVLpLK5fLFIoHHnHDYaSo1OotJoNVGtDqHRB8nqa1H9QayIA

### 💻 Code

```ts
type ReadA = <R>() => [false, R] | [true, R | undefined];
type ReadB = <R>() => [false, R] | [true, R | undefined];

// Error: Type 'ReadA' is not assignable to type 'ReadB'.
const test = (_: ReadA): ReadB => _;

// Also happens with object types
type ReadObjA = <R>() => { done: false; value: R } | { done: true; value: R | undefined };
type ReadObjB = <R>() => { done: false; value: R } | { done: true; value: R | undefined };

// Error: Type 'ReadObjA' is not assignable to type 'ReadObjB'.
const testObj = (_: ReadObjA): ReadObjB => _;
```


### 🙁 Actual behavior

The code fails to compile with error TS2322: Type 'ReadA' is not assignable to type 'ReadB'.

It appears that the compiler incorrectly widens the generic type parameter `R` in the source type.
Although `ReadA` is defined as `[false, R] | ...`, the error message reports the source type as having `[false, R | undefined]`.

It seems that during the generic signature assignability check, the undefined from the `[true, R | undefined]` branch is leaking into the inference of `R` for the entire union, causing the `false` branch to become `[false, R | undefined]`. This widened source type is then incompatible with the target's more strict `[false, R]` branch.

```
Type 'ReadA' is not assignable to type 'ReadB'.
  Type '[true, R | undefined] | [false, R | undefined]' is not assignable to type '[false, R] | [true, R | undefined]'.
    Type '[false, R | undefined]' is not assignable to type '[false, R] | [true, R | undefined]'.
      Type '[false, R | undefined]' is not assignable to type '[false, R]'.
        Type at position 1 in source is not compatible with type at position 1 in target.
          Type 'R | undefined' is not assignable to type 'R'.
            'R' could be instantiated with an arbitrary type which could be unrelated to 'R | undefined'.(2322)
```

```
Type 'ReadObjA' is not assignable to type 'ReadObjB'.
  Type '{ done: false; value: R | undefined; } | { done: true; value: R | undefined; }' is not assignable to type '{ done: false; value: R; } | { done: true; value: R | undefined; }'.
    Type '{ done: false; value: R | undefined; }' is not assignable to type '{ done: false; value: R; } | { done: true; value: R | undefined; }'.
      Type '{ done: false; value: R | undefined; }' is not assignable to type '{ done: false; value: R; }'.
        Types of property 'value' are incompatible.
          Type 'R | undefined' is not assignable to type 'R'.
            'R' could be instantiated with an arbitrary type which could be unrelated to 'R | undefined'.(2322)
```

### 🙂 Expected behavior

The code should compile without errors because `ReadA` and `ReadB` are structurally identical types.

### Acknowledgement

- [x] I acknowledge that issues using this template may be closed without further explanation at the maintainer's discretion.

### Comment

Hello TypeScript team,

I encountered a confusing and potentially misleading translation in the Chinese (`zh-CN`) diagnostic message for error **TS2561**.

**Current Chinese message:**  
> 对象字面量只能指定已知的属性，但“comprehensiveFilterTab”中不存在类型“PageState”。是否要写入 comprehensiveFilterList?

**Original English message:**  
> Object literal may only specify known properties, but 'comprehensiveFilterTab' does not exist in type 'PageState'. Did you mean to write 'comprehensiveFilterList'?

**Issue:**  
The Chinese translation says:  
> “但‘comprehensiveFilterTab’中不存在类型‘PageState’”  
which literally means “but type ‘PageState’ does not exist in ‘comprehensiveFilterTab’”.

This reverses the logical relationship and is **grammatically incorrect**, leading developers to misunderstand the error. It should convey that **the property `'comprehensiveFilterTab'` does not exist in the type `'PageState'`**, not the other way around.

**Suggested correction (Chinese):**  
> 对象字面量只能指定已知属性，但“comprehensiveFilterTab”在类型“PageState”中不存在。您是否想写“comprehensiveFilterList”？

This version preserves the original meaning and uses natural, unambiguous Chinese.

**How to reproduce:**  
Run `tsc --locale zh-CN` on code that triggers TS2561, e.g.:

```ts
type PageState = { comprehensiveFilterList: string[] };
const state: PageState = { comprehensiveFilterTab: [] }; // TS2561
```

Thank you for your attention! Accurate error messages are crucial for non-English developers.

body_text:
### Acknowledgement

- [x] I acknowledge that issues using this template may be closed without further explanation at the maintainer's discretion.

### Comment

In TypeScript 5 and below, `strict` was disabled by default. The `strict` option could be explained as a preset that enables certain options related stricter type checking, that weren’t enabled by default. I think for many users this option was analogous to _strict null checks and probably some other stuff_.

My take is practically akin to the above, but with a bit more nuance. When `strict` was introduced in [TypeScript 2.3](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-2-3.html), this was a preset that includes the 4 options `strictNullChecks`, `noImplicitAny`, `noImplicitThis`, and `alwaysStrict`. This strict mode came with the caveat that TypeScript might cause build failures, which many users have considered breaking changes in minor versions over the past years. In TypeScript 5, strict mode enabled 9 options.

The way I see it, strictness options follow several stages:

1. The option does not exist.
2. The option is introduced, but disabled by default.
3. The option is enabled if `strict` is enabled.
4. The option is enabled by default.

Maybe some stages are skipped. Maybe some stages are never reached.

---

In TypeScript 6, `strict` was changed to `true` by default. This was celebrated, because many people nowadays believe that these strict options are good. (And I agree!)

In my opinion however, this completely changed its meaning. This merges the stages 3 and 4. `strict` is no longer a preset to enable more strict options. Instead, it is now a preset you can use to enable 9 looser type checking options. You enable _loose_ mode by setting an option named _strict_ to _false_. You and I are aware how this came to be, but this is very weird to explain to new users. Understanding this option, requires understanding its history. Meanwhile, the explanations of the strict options are backwards. They state: _`true` if `strict`; `false` otherwise_. The real default is _`true` unless `strict` is set to `false`_. All reasoning about loose/strict mode now requires inverse reasoning. I also strongly believe there’s no point in having a loose mode at all.

In the age of LLMs this is even more confusing. Code review tools now confidently tell users they must enable `strict` because every blog post from before 2026 in its training data repeats this. But this information is outdated.

---

I believe that the `strict` should be either not exist or be repurposed to its old meaning.

For the option to not exist, that means:
- In a minor version:
  -  Deprecate `strict`
- In a major version
  - Decouple all related options from `strict`
  - Remove the `strict` option

For the option to be repurposed to its old meaning, that means:
- In a minor version:
  - Temporarily deprecate `strict`
- In a major version:
  - Decouple all currently related options from `strict`
  - Disable `strict` by default
  - Link new options to strict mode. I believe `verbatimModuleSyntax` is a good candidate.

In TypeScript 6, `strict` was changed to `true` by default. This was celebrated, because many people nowadays believe that these strict options are good. (And I agree!)

In my opinion however, this completely changed its meaning. This merges the stages 3 and 4. `strict` is no longer a preset to enable more strict options. Instead, it is now a preset you can use to enable 9 looser type checking options. You enable _loose_ mode by setting an option named _strict_ to _false_. You and I are aware how this came to be, but this is very weird to explain to new users. Understanding this option, requires understanding its history. Meanwhile, the explanations of the strict options are backwards. They state: _`true` if `strict`; `false` otherwise_. The real default is _`true` unless `strict` is set to `false`_. All reasoning about loose/strict mode now requires inverse reasoning. I also strongly believe there’s no point in having a loose mode at all.

In the age of LLMs this is even more confusing. Code review tools now confidently tell users they must enable `strict` because every blog post from before 2026 in its training data repeats this. But this information is outdated.

---

I believe that the `strict` should be either not exist or be repurposed to its old meaning.

For the option to not exist, that means:
- In a minor version:
  -  Deprecate `strict`
- In a major version
  - Decouple all related options from `strict`
  - Remove the `strict` option

For the option to be repurposed to its old meaning, that means:
- In a minor version:
  - Temporarily deprecate `strict`
- In a major version:
  - Decouple all currently related options from `strict`
  - Disable `strict` by default
  - Link new options to strict mode. I believe `verbatimModuleSyntax` is a good candidate.

### 🔍 Search Terms

"anonymous symbol properties"
"anonymous unique symbol"
"inline unique symbol"
"unique symbol property key"
"computed property unique symbol"
"symbol branding"

### ✅ Viability Checklist

- [x] This wouldn't be a breaking change in existing TypeScript/JavaScript code
- [x] This wouldn't change the runtime behavior of existing JavaScript code
- [x] This could be implemented without emitting different JS based on the types of the expressions
- [x] This isn't a runtime feature (e.g. library functionality, non-ECMAScript syntax with JavaScript output, new syntax sugar for JS, etc.)
- [x] This isn't a request to add a new utility type: https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/No-New-Utility-Types
- [x] This feature would agree with the rest of our Design Goals: https://github.com/Microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/TypeScript-Design-Goals

### ⭐ Suggestion

Allow `unique symbol` keys to be declared inline at the property declaration site.

### 📃 Motivating Example

**Current code:**
```ts
declare const brand: unique symbol;
type UserId = string & { readonly [brand]: "UserId" };
```

**Proposed code:**
```ts
type UserId = string & { readonly [brand: unique symbol]: "UserId" };
```

Each inline declaration would create a fresh symbol identity, equivalent to declaring a separate `unique symbol` and using it as the computed property key.
   
This is useful when a `unique symbol` property key is needed only once and does not need to be referenced independently. Common examples include phantom properties used for branded or refined types.

### 💻 Use Cases

1. What do you want to use this for?
   Declaring single-use `unique symbol` property keys inline, particularly for phantom properties used by branded or refined types.

2. What shortcomings exist with current approaches?
   The current approach requires introducing a value-level declaration solely to provide a unique identity for a type-level property key. For single-use symbol keys, this creates an otherwise unnecessary binding in the surrounding scope.

3. What workarounds are you using in the meantime?
   Declaring a separate `unique symbol` value and using it as a computed property key.

### 🔎 Search Terms

checkJs, allowJs, .d.mts, .d.cts, declaration file adjacent to implementation, file silently dropped from program, extension priority

### 🕗 Version & Regression Information

Reproduces identically on 5.9.3, 6.0.3, and 7.1.0-dev.20260916.1. Long-standing, not a regression.

### ⏯ Playground Link

Not applicable: needs two sibling files on disk plus `moduleResolution: nodenext`.

### 💻 Code

Three directories, identical but for extensions. Same `tsconfig.json` in each; `package.json` has `"type": "module"` only for the `.mjs` case.

`index.js` / `index.mjs` / `index.cjs`:

```js
export const n = 1;

const bad = null;
bad.a.b.c();
```

`index.d.ts` / `index.d.mts` / `index.d.cts`:

```ts
export declare const n: number;
```

```json
{
	"compilerOptions": {
		"target": "esnext",
		"module": "nodenext",
		"moduleResolution": "nodenext",
		"allowJs": true,
		"checkJs": true,
		"strict": true,
		"noEmit": true
	}
}
```

### 🙁 Actual behavior

```
index.js   + index.d.ts    ->  error TS18047: 'bad' is possibly 'null'.
index.mjs  + index.d.mts   ->  (no output)
index.cjs  + index.d.cts   ->  (no output)
```

The same authoring relationship — a hand-written declaration file beside its implementation — produces opposite outcomes based only on the file extension.

In the `.mjs`/`.cjs` cases the implementation is not merely unchecked, it is absent from the program: `--listFiles` reports only `index.d.mts`. In the `.js` case `--listFiles` reports both `index.d.ts` and `index.js`.

### 🙂 Expected behavior

The three rows should agree. Either all of them check the implementation, or none do.

I'd expect the `.js` row to be the correct one — the declaration file describes the module for consumers, and `checkJs` still checks the implementation — but consistency matters more than which way it goes.

### Additional information

#47796 reported the `.mjs`/`.mts` variant and was closed as "Working as Intended", on the rationale that the JS file is a build artifact of the TS file, and that "the compiler only automatically pulls in one copy of a file with the same basename (the most TS-y one)".

That rationale doesn't extend to this case:

- A `.d.mts` is not something a `.mjs` is emitted *from*, so the build-artifact framing doesn't apply. `.d.ts` + `.js` is the same relationship, and there the compiler does pull in both.
- Neither does the one-copy-per-basename rule, for the same reason — `index.js` and `index.d.ts` are both in the program.

The failure is silent, which is what makes it expensive: a package shipping `.mjs`/`.cjs` with adjacent hand-written declarations gets no checking of its implementation at all, while every sibling module without a declaration file is checked normally. `tsc` exits 0 and CI is green. I found this only by deliberately breaking a file and noticing the build still passed. Per #47796, VS Code *does* report these errors, so the editor and CI silently disagree.

#64098 is the same silent-drop shape from wildcard `include` (`hasFileWithHigherPriorityExtension`), if the two are related.

So, concretely:

1. Make the three rows consistent, or
2. if this is intended, document which sibling extensions suppress checking, and emit a diagnostic when an input file is dropped from the program for this reason.

### 🔍 Search Terms

fswatch

### ✅ Viability Checklist

- [x] This wouldn't be a breaking change in existing TypeScript/JavaScript code
- [x] This wouldn't change the runtime behavior of existing JavaScript code
- [x] This could be implemented without emitting different JS based on the types of the expressions
- [x] This isn't a runtime feature (e.g. library functionality, non-ECMAScript syntax with JavaScript output, new syntax sugar for JS, etc.)
- [x] This isn't a request to add a new utility type: https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/No-New-Utility-Types
- [x] This feature would agree with the rest of our Design Goals: https://github.com/Microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/TypeScript-Design-Goals

### ⭐ Suggestion

TypeScript developers have written a new nice `fswatch` Go package to watch filesystems. Good libraries are scarce in this domain.

Publishing `fswatch` as a stable, standalone Go package would allow others to rely on it and benefit the rest of the Go ecosystem. The package does _not_ need to be moved out of the TypeScript monorepo. The bare minimum would be to drop the "internal" flag, but it would be nicer for the package to have its own `go.mod` to reduce downstream dependencies.

### 📃 Motivating Example

I'm writing another Go tool which needs to listen to filesystem events.

### 💻 Use Cases

File synchronization programs, build tools, media galleries, and so on.

### 🔍 Search Terms

- protected alternative
- internal

Related issues:
- https://github.com/microsoft/typescript/issues/18499
- https://github.com/microsoft/typescript/issues/5228

### ✅ Viability Checklist

- [x] This wouldn't be a breaking change in existing TypeScript/JavaScript code
- [x] This wouldn't change the runtime behavior of existing JavaScript code
- [x] This could be implemented without emitting different JS based on the types of the expressions
- [x] This isn't a runtime feature (e.g. library functionality, non-ECMAScript syntax with JavaScript output, new syntax sugar for JS, etc.)
- [x] This isn't a request to add a new utility type: https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/No-New-Utility-Types
- [x] This feature would agree with the rest of our Design Goals: https://github.com/Microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/TypeScript-Design-Goals

### ⭐ Suggestion

Currently, `protected` causes several issues:
- you can't use duck typing when a class have a `protected` property. You can't implement it, you are required to extend it. 
- `protected` (and `private`) properties often disappear when manipulating types.

I'd like an `internal` modifier that would behave similarly to `readonly`.
It would declare the property is part of the public interface, but you can't access it outside of its methods (a.k.a. functions where the type of `this` is the type of the instance).

### 📃 Motivating Example

Such feature could be used for several usages.

**Having friends**

Currently, TS has no friend, even though this seems to be a frequently requested feature:
- https://github.com/microsoft/typescript/issues/7692
- https://github.com/microsoft/typescript/issues/35554

An `internal` modifier would be a cleaner way to have friends:
1. you declare a function/class with some internal properties.
2. you can safely cast such object by removing the `internal` modifier with some type manipulations (e.g. with `-internal`).

You can then select exactly which properties are accessibles from friends (which helps respecting encapsulation).

**Implementing classes with internal properties**

Sometimes we want to implement a class instead of extending it. However, this is not possible when using `protected` properties:
- https://github.com/microsoft/typescript/issues/61161

**Defining interfaces with internal properties**

We could also define interfaces with internal properties, e.g. hooks that could be overridden when extending a class implementing the interface, without even requiring to know the class true concrete type.

**Manipulating internal properties**

This would also enable more complex type manipulations, e.g.:
- https://github.com/microsoft/typescript/issues/46802

### 💻 Use Cases

Currently, there are several workarounds.

**Cast**

```ts
const internal = target as FooInternals;
```

Can be dangerous. A "type map" can be used to make the cast slightly more secure, but this is still unsafe.

**Public properties**

Making the properties public solves most of the issue, however, this makes properties publicly accessible, loosing some protections.

**Symbols**

We can hide the internal type behind a symbol.

```ts
class Foo {
      [SYMBOL] = this as InternalFoo;
      // or
       [SYMBOL] = { ... }
}
```

However, this is not ideal when manipulating classes in mixins (attributes aren't accessible from the prototype, and we can't really manipulate the constructor).

**Hooks in the constructor**

In some cases, you can give hooks in the base class constructor instead of overriding protected methods.

```ts
class Foo {
      [HOOKS]: XX; // not in the FooClass interface.

      constructor(hooks) {
             this[HOOKS] = hooks;
      }
}
```

But same as previously, this is not ideal when manipulating classes in mixins.

**Static properties**

Another way is to declare static instance methods that can be redefined:
```ts
class X {
      static onChange = () => {};
      foo() {
            this.constructor.onChange.call(this); // not type safe.
      }
}
```

However this is not truly type safe:
- https://github.com/microsoft/typescript/issues/3841

**Alternative suggestion :**

This issue could also be solved by specifying a public and an internal type for the same property:
- https://github.com/microsoft/typescript/issues/37487
- https://github.com/microsoft/typescript/issues/54829

The usage could then be something like `foo: $PUB_TYPE @internally=$INTERNAL_TYPE`, e.g.:
- `foo: never @internally=number`.
- `foo: readonly number @internally=number`.
- `foo: X @internally=XInternals`.

However this would require bigger changes to TS.

### ✅ Viability Checklist

- [x] This wouldn't change the runtime behavior of existing JavaScript code
- [x] This could be implemented without emitting different JS based on the types of the expressions

### ⭐ Suggestion

Currently, `protected` causes several issues:
- you can't use duck typing when a class have a `protected` property. You can't implement it, you are required to extend it. 
- `protected` (and `private`) properties often disappear when manipulating types.

I'd like an `internal` modifier that would behave similarly to `readonly`.
It would declare the property is part of the public interface, but you can't access it outside of its methods (a.k.a. functions where the type of `this` is the type of the instance).

### 📃 Motivating Example

Such feature could be used for several usages.

**Having friends**

Currently, TS has no friend, even though this seems to be a frequently requested feature:
- https://github.com/microsoft/typescript/issues/7692
- https://github.com/microsoft/typescript/issues/35554

An `internal` modifier would be a cleaner way to have friends:
1. you declare a function/class with some internal properties.
2. you can safely cast such object by removing the `internal` modifier with some type manipulations (e.g. with `-internal`).

You can then select exactly which properties are accessibles from friends (which helps respecting encapsulation).

**Implementing classes with internal properties**

Sometimes we want to implement a class instead of extending it. However, this is not possible when using `protected` properties:
- https://github.com/microsoft/typescript/issues/61161

**Defining interfaces with internal properties**

We could also define interfaces with internal properties, e.g. hooks that could be overridden when extending a class implementing the interface, without even requiring to know the class true concrete type.

**Manipulating internal properties**

This would also enable more complex type manipulations, e.g.:
- https://github.com/microsoft/typescript/issues/46802

### 💻 Use Cases

Currently, there are several workarounds.

**Cast**

```ts
const internal = target as FooInternals;
```

Can be dangerous. A "type map" can be used to make the cast slightly more secure, but this is still unsafe.

**Public properties**

Making the properties public solves most of the issue, however, this makes properties publicly accessible, loosing some protections.

**Symbols**

We can hide the internal type behind a symbol.

```ts
class Foo {
      [SYMBOL] = this as InternalFoo;
      // or
       [SYMBOL] = { ... }
}
```

However, this is not ideal when manipulating classes in mixins (attributes aren't accessible from the prototype, and we can't really manipulate the constructor).

**Hooks in the constructor**

In some cases, you can give hooks in the base class constructor instead of overriding protected methods.

```ts
class Foo {
      [HOOKS]: XX; // not in the FooClass interface.

      constructor(hooks) {
             this[HOOKS] = hooks;
      }
}
```

But same as previously, this is not ideal when manipulating classes in mixins.

**Static properties**

Another way is to declare static instance methods that can be redefined:
```ts
class X {
      static onChange = () => {};
      foo() {
            this.constructor.onChange.call(this); // not type safe.
      }
}
```

However this is not truly type safe:
- https://github.com/microsoft/typescript/issues/3841

**Alternative suggestion :**

This issue could also be solved by specifying a public and an internal type for the same property:
- https://github.com/microsoft/typescript/issues/37487
- https://github.com/microsoft/typescript/issues/54829

The usage could then be something like `foo: $PUB_TYPE @internally=$INTERNAL_TYPE`, e.g.:
- `foo: never @internally=number`.
- `foo: readonly number @internally=number`.
- `foo: X @internally=XInternals`.

### 🔎 Search Terms

Record<K1, T> & Record<K2, U>, generic Record intersection, mapped type intersection generic keys, K1 | K2, T & U

### 🕗 Version & Regression Information

- This is the behavior in every version I tried, and I reviewed the FAQ for entries about unsoundness


### ⏯ Playground Link

https://www.typescriptlang.org/play/?#code/MYewdgzgLgBAZjAvDAPAaQIwwKYA8rZgAmEM0ATgJZgDmANDACoNoBMO+hJZUVtDAVQB8ACgBQMGLgBcMAErZQ5IugwNGQmADJ5ikMvStBQumICUshUpWYYAHxht12mMKSbcYsaEixqABwBXKEs9AwAiAENwhgBvGDBZMECAWwAjbHIYAF9NHSt9FXC0mJh4lNkKahoczWR4yNl4xJgsbIY0ppgKmHDccJyc73BoGBBgoNhkOBQo0uak1Iys9t6SuO7K3mrakQDgs2HfTZ4+GuRxqEmAOkjrlLEgA

### 💻 Code

```ts
const f = <K1 extends string, T, K2 extends string, U>(
  x: Record<K1, T> & Record<K2, U>,
): Record<K1 | K2, T & U> => x

const input: Record<"a", { n: number }> & Record<"b", { m: string }> = { a: { n: 1 }, b: { m: "x" } }
const output = f<"a", { n: number }, "b", { m: string }>(input)
const m: string = output.a.m
```


### 🙁 Actual behavior

The return is accepted, and so is `output.a.m`. Key `"a"` is only present on `Record<"a", { n: number }>`, so its value is `{ n: 1 }`. The return type claims it is `{ n: number } & { m: string }`.

### 🙂 Expected behavior

The return should be an error. A key that belongs only to `K1` has type `T`, and `T` is not assignable to `T & U`. `output.a.m` should be an error.

Type: Feature Request I would like the tooltip that appears when hovering over the 'return' keyword in a function to display the type of the value returned by *that specific* `return` statement. The displayed information shouldn't necessarily be the inferred return type of the entire function (which is already visible by hovering over the function name) or the function's declared return type (if specified), but rather the type of the expression returned by *that specific* `return` statement. Example: ```ts function foo(val: number): string | number { if (Math.random() > .5) { return 42; // <- hovering over 'return' should display 'number' } else { return 'hello'; // <- hovering over 'return' should display 'string' } } ``` This would be very handy because, to get this inferred type information, I currently have to: 1) replace the 'return' keyword with 'const result =' 2) place the cursor after the expression 3) add a semicolon 4) enter a new line 5) add 'return result;' 6) hover over the 'result' variable to read the type 7) revert everything to how it was before Repeating this entire process every time I want to re-check the type is particularly tedious and cumbersome. ### 🔍 Search Terms

content mapper, contentMappers, extensionless import, extension-less import, custom file extension, extraExtensions, resolveHiddenExtensions, moduleSuffixes, bundler module resolution

### ✅ Viability Checklist

- [x] This wouldn't be a breaking change in existing TypeScript/JavaScript code
- [x] This wouldn't change the runtime behavior of existing JavaScript code
- [x] This could be implemented without emitting different JS based on the types of the expressions
- [x] This isn't a runtime feature (e.g. library functionality, non-ECMAScript syntax with JavaScript output, new syntax sugar for JS, etc.)
- [x] This isn't a request to add a new utility type: https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/No-New-Utility-Types
- [x] This feature would agree with the rest of our Design Goals: https://github.com/Microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/TypeScript-Design-Goals

### ⭐ Suggestion

Let the extensions registered in `contentMappers` take part in extensionless module lookup, after every built-in extension (`.ts`, `.tsx`, `.d.ts`, `.js`, `.jsx`), in the resolution modes that already add extensions (`bundler`, `node10`, and the CommonJS side of `node16`/`nodenext`).

```ts
// tsconfig.json: "contentMappers": [{ "package": "identity-foo-mapper", "extensions": [".foo"] }]
import { value } from "./card"; // today: TS2307; suggested: resolves to card.foo when no card.ts, card.tsx, card.d.ts, card.js or card.jsx exists
```

The mapper process plays no part in resolution. The resolver already reads the registered extension list to resolve fully specified imports such as `./card.foo` (the `extraExtensions` branch of `tryAddingExtensions`); this uses the same list in the extensionless branch. #64546 asked for this as a bug and is working as intended; this is the suggestion form.

A prototype against main at [`b85298b`](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/blob/b85298b6a81f772d080b0455de0ca9d744cd6fd6/tsc/internal/module/resolver.go#L1518-L1545):

```diff
--- a/tsc/internal/module/resolver.go
+++ b/tsc/internal/module/resolver.go
@@ -1542,6 +1542,16 @@ func (r *resolutionState) tryAddingExtensions(extensionless string, extensions e
 				return resolved
 			}
 		}
+		if originalExtension == "" && extensions&(extensionsTypeScript|extensionsDeclaration) != 0 && !r.isConfigLookup {
+			// Content-mapper extensions take part in extensionless lookup after every built-in
+			// candidate, so an existing .ts, .tsx, .d.ts, .js or .jsx file always wins.
+			for _, extension := range r.resolver.extraExtensions {
+				if resolved := r.tryExtension(extension, extensionless, false); !resolved.shouldContinueSearching() {
+					resolved.resolvedUsingExtraExtensions = true
+					return resolved
+				}
+			}
+		}
 		return continueSearching()
 	default:
 		if slices.Contains(r.resolver.extraExtensions, originalExtension) {
```

Results with the identity `.foo` mapper from #64546's reproduction, main vs. a local build of main with the prototype above:

| Case | main | prototype |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `./card` from a `.ts` file | TS2307 | resolves to `card.foo` |
| `./card` from a mapped `.foo` file | TS2307 | resolves to `card.foo` |
| `./card` with `moduleSuffixes: [".web", ""]` | TS2307 | resolves to `card.foo`: the compiler option puts the suffix after `.foo` (#64548). With the `moduleSuffixes` list on the `contentMappers` entry from #64560, resolves to `card.web.foo` |
| `./widgets` with `widgets/index.foo` | TS2307 | resolves to `widgets/index.foo` |
| `./card` with `card.ts` and `card.foo` | `card.ts` | `card.ts` |
| `./card` with `card.d.ts` and `card.foo` | `card.d.ts` | `card.d.ts` |

VS Code's built-in TypeScript extension lets other extensions send requests to its server with the `typescript.tsserverRequest` command: built-in requests from a short list, and any request whose name starts with `_` (a tsserver plugin can register those). Extensions for content-mapped languages need this, because several commands accept only TypeScript and JavaScript files.

The TypeScript 7 extension has no equivalent. The object its `activate` returns offers `registerContentMappers`, `onLanguageServerInitialized` and `initializeAPIConnection` (the native API, not the language server's requests), and no command forwards a request to `tsc --lsp`.

### Use cases

From TSRX (`.tsrx` files, served through a content mapper):

| Feature | VS Code's TypeScript (5.9 or 6) | TypeScript 7 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Go to Source Definition | TSRX's command sends `findSourceDefinition` through `typescript.tsserverRequest` (as a `_tsrx:` request that its tsserver plugin registers), and it works in `.tsrx` files | `tsc --lsp` answers `custom/textDocument/sourceDefinition` for content-mapped files, but the extension's command accepts only TypeScript and JavaScript language IDs (#64576), and no other extension can send the request |
| Find File References | same approach possible | not implemented yet (#63806); once it is, TSRX needs a way to ask for it on a `.tsrx` file |

With a way to send requests, an extension could offer these features for its own files without waiting for each command to accept content-mapped languages.

### Suggestion

A way for an extension to send a request to `tsc --lsp`, for example:

- `sendRequest(method, params, token)` on the API object, or
- a `typescript.native-preview.sendRequest` command, like `typescript.tsserverRequest`.

It could be limited to documents of the content mappers that the calling extension registered with `registerContentMappers`, or to `custom/*` methods.

Found while adding TypeScript 7 support for `.tsrx` files (https://github.com/tsrx-org/tsrx/issues/136).

extraFileExtensions

getDefaultProjectForFile
companion files
cold start project
openProjects




### ✅ Viability Checklist

- [x] This wouldn't be a breaking change in existing TypeScript/JavaScript code
- [x] This wouldn't change the runtime behavior of existing JavaScript code
- [x] This could be implemented without emitting different JS based on the types of the expressions
- [x] This isn't a runtime feature (e.g. library functionality, non-ECMAScript syntax with JavaScript output, new syntax sugar for JS, etc.)
- [x] This isn't a request to add a new utility type: https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/No-New-Utility-Types
- [x] This feature would agree with the rest of our Design Goals: https://github.com/Microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/TypeScript-Design-Goals

### ⭐ Suggestion

Something like content mappers for registering extra extensions as included in the project but without the requirement of actually doing content mapping

### 📃 Motivating Example

We're currently prototyping the new Angular Language Service against TS-Go (`tsgo --lsp` with the API session pipe). In our setup, our extension manages a separate language server to handle Angular-specific template features, and uses TS-Go as the backend semantic and type-checking engine.

Because we manage our own compiler instance per `tsconfig.json`, we need to know which project owns a file when it's opened. We're running into a cold-start discovery problem when a user opens an external template first (e.g. `app.component.html`): `getDefaultProjectForFile` returns nothing because TS doesn't recognize `.html` as belonging to any configured project. Since Angular hasn't compiled yet, we don't know the TS ↔ HTML association either, so we don't know which tsconfig to load.

To work around this today, we do a "fake open dance" where we guess a sibling `app.component.ts` file, send a synthetic `didOpen` to TS-Go just to spin up the project and discover the tsconfig path, and then boot our compiler.

Content Mappers don't really fit here because they require transforming foreign files into virtual `.ts` ASTs and generating `.ts` output. For Angular, HTML files are external companion templates—our template type-checking code is generated out-of-band in separate `.ngtypecheck.ts` files. Forcing a Content Mapper onto `.html` files just introduces unwanted `.ts` AST generation and emit overhead.

Previously, `extraFileExtensions` with `ScriptKind.Unknown` kept projects active when matched by `include` globs. Since non-TS extensions in `include` globs are more standard now with content mappers, we're fine requiring `.html` in `include`. A lightweight extension registration (or a no-transform companion mode that lets `include` globs associate `.html` with `ProjectService` without generating virtual `.ts` ASTs) would eliminate the cold-start issue and the fake open workaround.

### 💻 Use Cases

1. What do you want to use this for?
Angular language service

3. What shortcomings exist with current approaches?
Mentioned above

5. What workarounds are you using in the meantime?
attempting to open a ts file with the same name

- [x] This wouldn't change the runtime behavior of existing JavaScript code

- [x] This feature would agree with the rest of our Design Goals: https://github.com/Microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/TypeScript-Design-Goals

### ⭐ Suggestion

Something like content mappers for registering extra extensions as included in the project but without the requirement of actually doing content mapping

### 📃 Motivating Example

We're currently prototyping the new Angular Language Service against TS-Go (`tsgo --lsp` with the API session pipe). In our setup, our extension manages a separate language server to handle Angular-specific template features, and uses TS-Go as the backend semantic and type-checking engine.

Because we manage our own compiler instance per `tsconfig.json`, we need to know which project owns a file when it's opened. We're running into a cold-start discovery problem when a user opens an external template first (e.g. `app.component.html`): `getDefaultProjectForFile` returns nothing because TS doesn't recognize `.html` as belonging to any configured project. Since Angular hasn't compiled yet, we don't know the TS ↔ HTML association either, so we don't know which tsconfig to load.

To work around this today, we do a "fake open dance" where we guess a sibling `app.component.ts` file, send a synthetic `didOpen` to TS-Go just to spin up the project and discover the tsconfig path, and then boot our compiler.

Content Mappers don't really fit here because they require transforming foreign files into virtual `.ts` ASTs and generating `.ts` output. For Angular, HTML files are external companion templates—our template type-checking code is generated out-of-band in separate `.ngtypecheck.ts` files. Forcing a Content Mapper onto `.html` files just introduces unwanted `.ts` AST generation and emit overhead.

Previously, `extraFileExtensions` with `ScriptKind.Unknown` kept projects active when matched by `include` globs. Since non-TS extensions in `include` globs are more standard now with content mappers, we're fine requiring `.html` in `include`. A lightweight extension registration (or a no-transform companion mode that lets `include` globs associate `.html` with `ProjectService` without generating virtual `.ts` ASTs) would eliminate the cold-start issue and the fake open workaround.

### Acknowledgement

- [x] I acknowledge that issues using this template may be closed without further explanation at the maintainer's discretion.

### Comment

### 🔎 Search Terms

class name eval arguments, class arguments strict mode, TS1210 class name, TS1215 class declaration, checkStrictModeEvalOrArguments class

### 🕗 Version & Regression Information

- This is the behavior in every version I tried (4.0.8, 5.0.4, 6.0.2, 7.1.0-dev.20261006.1), and I reviewed the FAQ for entries about strict mode and reserved words

### ⏯ Playground Link

https://www.typescriptlang.org/play/?ts=6.0.0-dev.20260416#

### 💻 Code

```ts
class arguments {}        // no error, expected TS1210
class eval {}             // no error, expected TS1210
const C = class eval {};  // no error, expected TS1210
declare class eval {} // no error, expected TS1210

// For comparison, all other strict-mode bindings are reported:
function f() {
  class D { m(arguments: number) {} } // TS1210
}
export {};
```

### 🙁 Actual behavior

No errors are reported for the class names. The emitted JavaScript is rejected at runtime:

```sh
$ node out.js
SyntaxError: Unexpected eval or arguments in strict mode
```

The same happens in a `.js` file with `checkJs` enabled.

### 🙂 Expected behavior

Each class name `eval` / `arguments` should be reported, as other strict mode bindings already are. Per the spec, all parts of a class are strict mode code ([ECMA-262 §11.2.2](https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-strict-mode-code)), and it is an early error for a `BindingIdentifier` in strict mode code to be `eval` or `arguments` ([§13.1.1](https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-identifiers-static-semantics-early-errors)). This applies to both class declarations and class expressions.

### Additional information about the issue

In the binder, function names (`checkStrictModeFunctionName`), variable declarations (`bindVariableDeclarationOrBindingElement`) and parameters (`bindParameter`) all call `checkStrictModeEvalOrArguments`. `bindClassLikeDeclaration` never does, so class names skip this check.

`bindWorker` already sets `inStrictMode = true` for `ClassDeclaration` / `ClassExpression` before it calls `bindClassLikeDeclaration`. So a fix could follow `checkStrictModeFunctionName`: call `checkStrictModeEvalOrArguments(node, node.name)` in `bindClassLikeDeclaration` when not in an ambient context.

Found this issue while fixing the same bug in Babel's parser: https://github.com/babel/babel/pull/18315

### 🔎 Search Terms DeepCloneNode, conditionalTypeToTypeNode, declaration emit out of memory, recursive conditional type, non-exported type alias, TS7056, watch mode memory, noEmit watch ### 🕗 Version & Regression Information - Reproduces on `7.0.2` and on `7.1.0-dev.20261009.1` (macOS, arm64). - Not yet compared with 6.0. ### ⏯ Playground Link Needs two modules (the helper aliases must live in another file and stay unexported), so the repro is below. ### 💻 Code ```ts // types.ts type Tail = T extends [unknown, ...infer R] ? R : []; type Shift = P[0] extends K ? Tail

: never; type NonUndefined = T extends undefined ? never : T; type Rec = T extends object ? { [K in Extract]: NonUndefined>> } : T; export type Expanded = Rec; export interface Entity { id: string } ``` ```ts // api.ts import type { Entity, Expanded } from "./types"; declare function get(): T; export const fetch =

() => get>(); ``` ```json // tsconfig.json { "compilerOptions": { "strict": true, "declaration": true, "emitDeclarationOnly": true, "outDir": "out", "types": [] }, "files": ["types.ts", "api.ts"] } ``` Run `tsc -p .` ### 🙁 Actual behavior The compiler never finishes. Memory passes 3 GB within about 5 seconds and keeps growing until the process is killed. On a real project with the same pattern in 11 modules, a full declaration emit reached 52 GB in 3.5 minutes before we stopped it. The same thing happens in a project that never asks for declarations, through watch mode. With `"noEmit": true` instead of the declaration options, and a third file importing `fetch` from `./api`: 1. `tsc -p . --watch` completes the initial build normally (about 90 MB, `Found 0 errors`). 2. Append a comment to `api.ts`. 3. The watcher starts declaration emit for the changed file and grows without bound (3 GB after 5 to 7 seconds in this repro). In our project the watcher reached a 65 GB footprint. A plain `tsc -p . --noEmit` is fine (about 100 MB). Sampled stack (symbolized from the release binary, condensed): ``` compiler.(*Program).Emit.func2 compiler.(*emitter).emitDeclarationFile transformers/declarations.(*DeclarationTransformer).transformVariableDeclaration transformers/declarations.(*DeclarationTransformer).ensureType checker.(*NodeBuilderImpl).serializeTypeForDeclaration checker.(*NodeBuilderImpl).serializeReturnTypeForSignature checker.(*NodeBuilderImpl).typeToTypeNode checker.(*NodeBuilderImpl).createMappedTypeNodeFromType checker.(*NodeBuilderImpl).conditionalTypeToTypeNode (repeats) ast.(*NodeFactory).DeepCloneNode ast.(*ConditionalTypeNode).VisitEachChild (very deep) ast.(*IndexedAccessTypeNode).VisitEachChild ``` Most of the remaining CPU time goes to GC (`scanObject`, `findObject`) and map lookups under `printer.(*EmitContext).SetOriginalEx`. ### 🙂 Expected behavior Emit terminates, either with a truncated type or with TS7056. The nightly already does that for close variants of this repro: | Variant | 7.0.2 | 7.1.0-dev.20261009.1 | |---|---|---| | Repro as above | runaway | runaway | | Without the `NonUndefined<...>` wrapper | finishes, writes a 2.5 MB `api.d.ts` | TS7056, about 30 MB | | `Rec` instead of `Rec>` | finishes, writes a 660 KB `api.d.ts` | TS7056, about 30 MB | | Helper aliases exported | about 30 MB, 220 byte `api.d.ts` | about 30 MB, 220 byte `api.d.ts` | ### Additional information about the issue - Workaround: export the helper aliases. The printer can then reference `import("./types").Rec<...>` instead of inlining the alias body into itself. - The real world shape is a common "make these dotted paths required" helper (`DeepRequiredObj` with a path to tuple split), used as the type argument of a generic API client method without an explicit return type. - Possibly related: #63825 (closed without a repro, same `DeepCloneNode` runaway on the declaration emit path), #63966 / #63969, #64556. The nightly includes those fixes and still reproduces this one. - The watch mode part seems worth noting on its own: a `noEmit` project can run into declaration emit problems just by saving a file, because the builder computes `.d.ts` signatures for changed files.

### 🔎 Search Terms

incremental stale diagnostics declare global augmentation node_modules types tsbuildinfo

### 🕗 Version & Regression Information

- This changed between versions 6.0.3 and 7.0.2.
- 7.0.2: the change is not found. 6.0.3: the change is found.
- Also wrong on 5.6.1-rc. Tested on macOS arm64, Node.js 24.20.0.

### ⏯ Playground Link

None: the bug needs `--incremental` and a package in `node_modules`. The script below makes the 5 files and runs the steps.

### 💻 Code

A package declares a type in a `declare global` block of a module declaration file. The project loads the package with `types`, and does not import it.

```ts
// app/node_modules/pkg/package.json
{ "name": "pkg", "version": "1.0.0", "types": "index.d.ts" }

// app/node_modules/pkg/index.d.ts
import './globals.js'
export {}

// app/node_modules/pkg/globals.d.ts
declare global {
    namespace NS {
        interface M { f(x: string): void }
    }
}
export {}

// app/tsconfig.json
{ "compilerOptions": { "strict": true, "module": "nodenext", "noEmit": true, "types": ["pkg"] }, "files": ["test.ts"] }

// app/test.ts
declare const m: NS.M
m.f('a')
export {}
```

Script (run it in an empty folder where `npx tsc` is the version to test):

```sh
mkdir -p repro/pkg repro/app/node_modules && cd repro
printf '{ "name": "pkg", "version": "1.0.0", "types": "index.d.ts" }\n' > pkg/package.json
printf "import './globals.js'\nexport {}\n" > pkg/index.d.ts
printf 'declare global {\n    namespace NS {\n        interface M { f(x: string): void }\n    }\n}\nexport {}\n' > pkg/globals.d.ts
cp -R pkg app/node_modules/pkg
printf '{ "compilerOptions": { "strict": true, "module": "nodenext", "noEmit": true, "types": ["pkg"] }, "files": ["test.ts"] }\n' > app/tsconfig.json
printf "declare const m: NS.M\nm.f('a')\nexport {}\n" > app/test.ts
cd app
npx tsc --noEmit --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile ../app.tsbuildinfo -p tsconfig.json && echo "1. incremental: no error"
sed -i.bak 's/f(x: string)/f(x: number)/' node_modules/pkg/globals.d.ts
npx tsc --noEmit --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile ../app.tsbuildinfo -p tsconfig.json && echo "2. incremental after the change: no error (wrong)"
npx tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json || echo "3. clean build after the change: TS2345 (correct)"
```

Steps:
1. `tsc --noEmit --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile ../app.tsbuildinfo -p tsconfig.json`: no error (expected).
2. In `globals.d.ts`, change `f(x: string)` to `f(x: number)`, and run step 1 again with the same build info file.
3. Run `tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json`, with no build info file.

### 🙁 Actual behavior

With 7.0.2, step 2 reports no error. Step 3 reports:

```text
test.ts(2,5): error TS2345: Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'number'.
```

The incremental build and the clean build disagree on the same files. The result is the same with `skipLibCheck: true`, and when `node_modules/pkg` is a symlink to the package.

### 🙂 Expected behavior

Step 2 reports the TS2345 error, as the clean build does, and as 6.0.3 does in step 2.

### Additional information about the issue

- Related, but not the same: #64386 (stale diagnostics with a module augmentation through a re-export, inside the project), #64552 (stale diagnostics after a change of `lib` or `target`, 7.0.2). Older: #44094, fixed by #45156.
- Found in the type tests of [expect-webdriverio](https://github.com/webdriverio/expect-webdriverio): its global `expect` and the `ExpectWebdriverIO` namespace come from a `declare global` block in a module declaration file of the package. Vitest runs its type tests with `tsc --noEmit --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile <vitest>/dist/tsconfig.tmp.tsbuildinfo`, so a broken public type gave 141 passed tests, while a clean `tsc` found 22 errors. Workaround: delete the build info file before each run (webdriverio/expect-webdriverio#2357).

{"repository": "microsoft/TypeScript", "task_candidate_id": 11735, "repository_id": 169, "issue_number": 64715, "github_issue_id": 5787054825, "html_url": "https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/issues/64715", "created_at": "2026-10-10T01:58:09+00:00", "author_association": null, "title": "`--incremental` keeps stale diagnostics after a change in a `declare global` block of a package declaration file (7.0.2, regression from 6.0.3)", "body_text": "### 🔎 Search Terms

incremental stale diagnostics declare global augmentation node_modules types tsbuildinfo

### 🕗 Version & Regression Information

- This changed between versions 6.0.3 and 7.0.2.
- 7.0.2: the change is not found. 6.0.3: the change is found.
- Also wrong on 5.6.1-rc. Tested on macOS arm64, Node.js 24.20.0.

### ⏯ Playground Link

None: the bug needs `--incremental` and a package in `node_modules`. The script below makes the 5 files and runs the steps.

### 💻 Code

A package declares a type in a `declare global` block of a module declaration file. The project loads the package with `types`, and does not import it.

```ts
// app/node_modules/pkg/package.json
{ "name": "pkg", "version": "1.0.0", "types": "index.d.ts" }

// app/node_modules/pkg/index.d.ts
import './globals.js'
export {}

// app/node_modules/pkg/globals.d.ts
declare global {
    namespace NS {
        interface M { f(x: string): void }
    }
}
export {}

// app/tsconfig.json
{ "compilerOptions": { "strict": true, "module": "nodenext", "noEmit": true, "types": ["pkg"] }, "files": ["test.ts"] }

// app/test.ts
declare const m: NS.M
m.f('a')
export {}
```

Script (run it in an empty folder where `npx tsc` is the version to test):

```sh
mkdir -p repro/pkg repro/app/node_modules && cd repro
printf '{ "name": "pkg", "version": "1.0.0", "types": "index.d.ts" }\n' > pkg/package.json
printf "import './globals.js'\nexport {}\n" > pkg/index.d.ts
printf 'declare global {\n    namespace NS {\n        interface M { f(x: string): void }\n    }\n}\nexport {}\n' > pkg/globals.d.ts
cp -R pkg app/node_modules/pkg
printf '{ "compilerOptions": { "strict": true, "module": "nodenext", "noEmit": true, "types": ["pkg"] }, "files": ["test.ts"] }\n' > app/tsconfig.json
printf "declare const m: NS.M\nm.f('a')\nexport {}\n" > app/test.ts
cd app
npx tsc --noEmit --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile ../app.tsbuildinfo -p tsconfig.json && echo "1. incremental: no error"
sed -i.bak 's/f(x: string)/f(x: number)/' node_modules/pkg/globals.d.ts
npx tsc --noEmit --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile ../app.tsbuildinfo -p tsconfig.json && echo "2. incremental after the change: no error (wrong)"
npx tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json || echo "3. clean build after the change: TS2345 (correct)"
```

Steps:
1. `tsc --noEmit --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile ../app.tsbuildinfo -p tsconfig.json`: no error (expected).
2. In `globals.d.ts`, change `f(x: string)` to `f(x: number)`, and run step 1 again with the same build info file.
3. Run `tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json`, with no build info file.

### 🙁 Actual behavior

With 7.0.2, step 2 reports no error. Step 3 reports:

```text
test.ts(2,5): error TS2345: Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'number'.
```

The incremental build and the clean build disagree on the same files. The result is the same with `skipLibCheck: true`, and when `node_modules/pkg` is a symlink to the package.

### 🙂 Expected behavior

Step 2 reports the TS2345 error, as the clean build does, and as 6.0.3 does in step 2.

### Additional information about the issue

- Related, but not the same: #64386 (stale diagnostics with a module augmentation through a re-export, inside the project), #64552 (stale diagnostics after a change of `lib` or `target`, 7.0.2). Older: #44094, fixed by #45156.
- Found in the type tests of [expect-webdriverio](https://github.com/webdriverio/expect-webdriverio): its global `expect` and the `ExpectWebdriverIO` namespace come from a `declare global` block in a module declaration file of the package. Vitest runs its type tests with `tsc --noEmit --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile <vitest>/dist/tsconfig.tmp.tsbuildinfo`, so a broken public type gave 141 passed tests, while a clean `tsc` found 22 errors. Workaround: delete the build info file before each run (webdriverio/expect-webdriverio#2357).

### 🔎 Search Terms

noEmit declaration diagnostics, TS2527, inaccessible this type, TypeScript 7 noEmit declaration

### 🕗 Version & Regression Information

- This changed between versions 6.0.3 and 7.0.2 (also reproduces with `@typescript/native-preview` 7.0.0-dev.20260707.2)
- Not listed in `tsc/CHANGES.md`, `submoduleAccepted.txt` or `submoduleTriaged.txt`

### ⏯ Playground Link

(not applicable: depends on the `--noEmit` + `--declaration` CLI combination)

### 💻 Code

```ts
// repro.ts
const n: number = "oops";   // any ordinary semantic error

class C4 {
    x1 = { a: this };       // declaration-emit diagnostic TS2527
}
```

```
tsc --target es2015 --noEmit --declaration true repro.ts
```

### 🙁 Actual behavior

TypeScript 7.0.2 reports both diagnostics under `--noEmit`:

```
repro.ts(1,7): error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.
repro.ts(4,5): error TS2527: The inferred type of 'x1' references an inaccessible 'this' type. A type annotation is necessary.
```

TypeScript 6.0.3 reports only the semantic error under `--noEmit`:

```
repro.ts(1,7): error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.
```

The two compilers agree in every other combination I tried: with actual emit (`--declaration true --outDir out`) both report TS2527, and when the file has **no** other semantic error both report TS2527 even under `--noEmit`. So the difference is specifically: *under `--noEmit`, TS 6 skips declaration-emit diagnostics when semantic errors are present, TS 7 does not.*

### 🙂 Expected behavior

Either identical output to 6.0.3 under `--noEmit` (the 7.0 announcement states that type-checking and CLI behaviour should match 6.0), or, if reporting declaration diagnostics under `--noEmit` regardless of semantic errors is intentional, an entry in `tsc/CHANGES.md`. Projects that type-check with `tsc --noEmit` in CI while keeping `"declaration": true` in tsconfig will see new errors after upgrading only when some other error is present, which is confusing to diagnose.

### Additional information about the issue

Found by running `tests/cases/conformance/types/thisType/declarationFiles.ts` through `tsc6` and `tsc` (7.0.2) with the test's own `// @declaration: true` directive and `--noEmit`: 6.0.3 reports 13 errors, 7.0.2 reports 17 (the four TS2527 lines). Across the 4,552 single-file conformance tests this was the only difference not already covered by `submoduleAccepted.txt` or by a referenced issue.

### Acknowledgement

- [x] I acknowledge that issues using this template may be closed without further explanation at the maintainer's discretion.

### Comment

In TypeScript 6 a conditional type has `root: ConditionalRoot` (public in `typescript.d.ts`), and `root.node` is the `ConditionalTypeNode` it was declared with. In the TypeScript 7 API, `ConditionalType` has `getCheckType()`, `getExtendsType()`, `getTrueType()` and `getFalseType()`, and nothing that leads to that node. For an instantiated conditional type without an alias symbol I have found no way to get its branches as they were declared.

```ts
declare class Box<T, V> {
  get(): T extends string ? V : never;
}
export function h<U>(box: Box<U, { a: number }>) {
  return box.get();
}
```

For the type of `box.get()`, which prints as `U extends string ? { a: number; } : never` in both versions:

| | TypeScript 6.0.3 | TypeScript 7.0.2 (`typescript/unstable/sync`) |
|---|---|---|

### 🔎 Search Terms

tsc --lsp exit code 1, shutdown exit, context canceled, handleExit io.EOF, LSP exit notification

### 🕗 Version & Regression Information

- I was unable to test this on prior versions because `--lsp` is new in TypeScript 7: seen with `typescript` 7.0.2 (`tsc --lsp --stdio`), macOS arm64. I have not run the nightly; the code path below is unchanged on `main` at aa81492.

### ⏯ Playground Link

_No response_ (language server, not type checking)

### 💻 Code

Save as `repro.py` and run `python3 repro.py` in any directory. It initializes `tsc --lsp --stdio`, sends `shutdown`, then `exit`, and prints the exit code (given a URI, it opens a document first; no argument opens nothing).

```python
# python3 repro.py [URI to open], in a directory with a tsconfig.json
import json, os, subprocess, sys

p = subprocess.Popen(["tsc", "--lsp", "--stdio"], stdin=subprocess.PIPE, stdout=subprocess.PIPE)

def send(msg):
    body = json.dumps({"jsonrpc": "2.0", **msg}).encode()
    p.stdin.write(b"Content-Length: %d\r\n\r\n%s" % (len(body), body))
    p.stdin.flush()

def reply(id):
    while True:
        length = None
        while (line := p.stdout.readline()) not in (b"\r\n", b""):
            if line.lower().startswith(b"content-length:"):
                length = int(line.split(b":")[1])
        if length is None:
            return None  # the server is gone
        msg = json.loads(p.stdout.read(length))
        if "method" in msg and "id" in msg:  # a request from the server
            send({"id": msg["id"], "result": None})
        elif msg.get("id") == id:
            return msg

root = "file://" + os.getcwd()
send({"id": 1, "method": "initialize", "params": {"processId": os.getpid(), "rootUri": root, "capabilities": {}}})
reply(1)
send({"method": "initialized", "params": {}})
if len(sys.argv) > 1:
    doc = {"uri": sys.argv[1], "languageId": "typescript", "version": 0, "text": "const x = 1;\n"}
    send({"method": "textDocument/didOpen", "params": {"textDocument": doc}})
send({"id": 2, "method": "shutdown"})
if reply(2) is not None:
    send({"method": "exit"})
print("exit code:", p.wait())
```

### 🙁 Actual behavior

```
$ python3 repro.py
context canceled
exit code: 1
```

The server exits with code 1 after a clean `shutdown` and `exit`. Neovim reports any non-zero exit, so every `:lsp restart` shows "Client tsc quit with exit code 1 and signal 0. Check log for errors".

Reading `main` at aa81492, the path looks like this:

- [`handleExit`](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/blob/aa8149273b23401f0a79a5f0384c42de51888693/tsc/internal/lsp/server.go#L1836-L1838) returns `io.EOF`.
- [`dispatchLoop`](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/blob/aa8149273b23401f0a79a5f0384c42de51888693/tsc/internal/lsp/server.go#L1004-L1032) answers that with `lspExit(nil)`, which cancels the loop's context.
- Its next `s.requestQueue.Get(ctx)` then returns `context.Canceled`, and the loop returns that.
- [`Run`](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/blob/aa8149273b23401f0a79a5f0384c42de51888693/tsc/internal/lsp/server.go#L913) passes it on, since it isn't `io.EOF` and the group's context is done.
- [`cmd/tsc/lsp.go`](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/blob/aa8149273b23401f0a79a5f0384c42de51888693/tsc/cmd/tsc/lsp.go#L71-L73) prints it and returns 1.

### 🙂 Expected behavior

Exit code 0: the LSP spec asks for 0 when `shutdown` came before `exit`, and 1 otherwise.
