### 🔎 Search Terms

documentHighlight, document highlight, URI encoding, percent-encoding, %40, @ in path, Neovim, LSP

### 🕗 Version & Regression Information

- I was unable to test this on prior versions because this code is in the TS7 language server only. The old tsserver (through vtsls) does not have this problem.

I reproduced it with `tsc --lsp` 7.0.2. The same code is on `main` at ba1819f.

### ⏯ Playground Link

Not applicable. The problem is in the language server.

### 💻 Code

Put this file in a directory whose path contains `@`, for example `/tmp/a@b/proj/x.ts`, with an empty `tsconfig.json` next to it:

```ts
const foo = 1;
console.log(foo);
console.log(foo);
```

### 🙁 Actual behavior

`textDocument/documentHighlight` on `foo` (line 0, character 7) returns an empty array if the client sends the path with `@` not encoded:

| URI that the client sends     | Highlights |
| ----------------------------- | ---------- |
| `file:///tmp/a@b/proj/x.ts`   | 0          |
| `file:///tmp/a%40b/proj/x.ts` | 3          |
| `file:///tmp/plain/proj/x.ts` | 3          |

Neovim sends the first form (`vim.uri_from_fname("/tmp/a@b/x.ts")` gives `file:///tmp/a@b/x.ts`). Thus, in Neovim, document highlights and features that use them (for example, jump to next reference) do not work in projects whose path contains `@`. Other requests, such as `textDocument/references`, work correctly on the same file.

### 🙂 Expected behavior

The server returns 3 highlights for all three URIs. The two `a@b` URIs identify the same file, and the server opens that file correctly from both forms.

### Additional information about the issue

**Cause.** `tsc/internal/ls/documenthighlights.go:30` filters the results with a raw string compare:

```go
if mh.Uri == documentUri {
```

- `mh.Uri` comes from `lsconv.FileNameToDocumentURI`, which encodes `@` as `%40` (`tsc/internal/ls/lsconv/converters.go:315`).
- `documentUri` is the string that the client sent, without changes.

When the client does not encode `@`, the strings are different, and the filter removes all highlights. VS Code does not see this problem because `vscode-uri` also encodes `@` as `%40` (`URI.file('/tmp/a@b/x.ts').toString()` gives `file:///tmp/a%40b/x.ts`). Thus the two sides always agree.

**Why this is a server problem.** RFC 3986 permits `@` in a path segment without encoding, so the client URI is valid. Also, the LSP specification ([URI section](https://microsoft.github.io/language-server-protocol/specifications/lsp/3.17/specification/#uri)) says:

> Clients and servers should not assume that each other are encoding the same way (for example a client encoding colons in drive letters cannot assume server responses will have encoded colons).

**Possible fix.** Compare file names, not URI strings:

```go
if mh.Uri.FileName() == documentUri.FileName() {
```

Another possible fix is to normalize `documentUri` one time before the loop. Other characters in `extraEscapeReplacer` (`'`, `(`, `)`, `*`, `+`, `,`, `;`, `=`, `!`, `$`, `&`, and so on) probably cause the same problem with clients that do not encode them.

Related: #43261 had the same type of cause (a path-case mismatch caused document highlights to fail) in tsserver.

**Environment**

- Neovim v0.12.0-dev, Linux (WSL2)
- `tsc --lsp` 7.0.2

### Version and platform

`typescript@7.0.2` native compiler, package `gitHead` `2bd066d87f5bafd315be9f40889d0a60b9e58e0b`, macOS arm64.

### Crash

A real stdio LSP session checks a program and its relative helper successfully, checks the changed helper's type error successfully, then crashes while the client closes documents and shuts the server down. The client does not advertise dynamic file-watch registration, so the server uses its internal watcher. This reproduced in three focused local runs, including a client that flushes the exit frame, closes stdin, and waits for the owned process.

```text
panic: assignment to entry in nil map [recovered, repanicked]

github.com/microsoft/typescript-go/internal/lsp/lspwatcher.(*Watcher).WatchFiles
    internal/lsp/lspwatcher/lspwatcher.go:160
github.com/microsoft/typescript-go/internal/lsp.(*Server).WatchFiles
    internal/lsp/server.go:232
github.com/microsoft/typescript-go/internal/project.updateWatch
    internal/project/session.go:1271
github.com/microsoft/typescript-go/internal/project.(*Session).updateWatches
    internal/project/session.go:1394
github.com/microsoft/typescript-go/internal/project.(*Session).updateSnapshot.func1
    internal/project/session.go:1234
github.com/microsoft/typescript-go/internal/project/background.(*Queue).Enqueue.func1
    internal/project/background/queue.go:38
```

The strict client-side lifecycle check observes `tsgo --lsp --stdio: exit status 2`; this is not a passed shutdown.

### Source race

At the exact revision, `WatchFiles` marks its id while holding `w.mu`, releases that lock while installing a new subscription, then reacquires it and appends to `w.watches[id]`. `Close` can run in between: it sets `closed = true` and `w.watches = nil`. The post-install publication does not recheck `closed` before assigning into the map.

Source: https://github.com/microsoft/typescript-go/blob/2bd066d87f5bafd315be9f40889d0a60b9e58e0b/internal/lsp/lspwatcher/lspwatcher.go#L125-L161

### Proposed fix and deterministic control

Recheck `closed` under `w.mu` immediately before publishing the installed subscription. If closed, unlock, close the unpublished subscription, and return the existing `lspwatcher: closed` error. Do not suppress the panic or disable real watcher behavior.

A deterministic regression can use the existing watcher backend test seam: install a subscription, pause before `WatchDirectory` returns, call `Watcher.Close`, release the installer, and observe completion. It must return the closed error, close the unpublished subscription exactly once, and retain no watch. A paired arm with no concurrent close must still register normally. The schedule uses channel handshakes, not timing sleeps.

Local acceptance keeps the real cold/warm relative-module checks and the strict compiler-exit assertion; a shutdown panic is not tolerated as an expected success. The carried source patch remains tied to this revision until an upstream fixed publication is consumed.

The strict client-side lifecycle check observes `tsgo --lsp --stdio: exit status 2`; this is not a passed shutdown.

### Source race

At the exact revision, `WatchFiles` marks its id while holding `w.mu`, releases that lock while installing a new subscription, then reacquires it and appends to `w.watches[id]`. `Close` can run in between: it sets `closed = true` and `w.watches = nil`. The post-install publication does not recheck `closed` before assigning into the map.

Source: https://github.com/microsoft/typescript-go/blob/2bd066d87f5bafd315be9f40889d0a60b9e58e0b/internal/lsp/lspwatcher/lspwatcher.go#L125-L161

### Proposed fix and deterministic control

Recheck `closed` under `w.mu` immediately before publishing the installed subscription. If closed, unlock, close the unpublished subscription, and return the existing `lspwatcher: closed` error. Do not suppress the panic or disable real watcher behavior.

A deterministic regression can use the existing watcher backend test seam: install a subscription, pause before `WatchDirectory` returns, call `Watcher.Close`, release the installer, and observe completion. It must return the closed error, close the unpublished subscription exactly once, and retain no watch. A paired arm with no concurrent close must still register normally. The schedule uses channel handshakes, not timing sleeps.

Local acceptance keeps the real cold/warm relative-module checks and the strict compiler-exit assertion; a shutdown panic is not tolerated as an expected success. The carried source patch remains tied to this revision until an upstream fixed publication is consumed.

### 🔎 Search Terms

importModuleSpecifier, importModuleSpecifierEnding, importModuleSpecifierPreference, auto import, specifier cache, preference change, settings change not applied

### 🕗 Version & Regression Information

- TypeScript 7 native preview, `7.1.0-dev.20261014.1`

### ⏯ Playground Link

_No response_

### 💻 Code

```jsonc
// tsconfig.json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "esnext",
    "paths": { "~/*": ["./src/*"] }
  }
}
```

```ts
// src/util/path.ts
export const somePath = 10;
```

```ts
// src/util/index.ts
s
```

### 🙁 Actual behavior

1. Open `src/util/index.ts` and request completions after `s`. `somePath` is offered with the specifier `./path`.
2. Change `js/ts.preferences.importModuleSpecifier` to `"non-relative"`.
3. Request completions again in the same file. `somePath` is still offered with `./path`.

The same happens when changing `js/ts.preferences.importModuleSpecifierEnding`. Closing and reopening the file picks up the new setting.

### 🙂 Expected behavior

After the setting changes, completions in the open file should use the new preference: `~/util/path` for `"non-relative"`, and `./path.js` for `importModuleSpecifierEnding: "js"`.

### Additional information about the issue

`Registry.specifierCache` in `tsc/internal/ls/autoimport/registry.go` caches module specifiers per importing file, but does not record the preferences they were computed with. When user preferences change, the cache is only cleared if `autoImportSpecifierExcludeRegexes` changed, so specifiers computed with the previous `importModuleSpecifierPreference` or `importModuleSpecifierEnding` keep being returned for files that are already open.

### 🔍 Search Terms

jujutsu, jj

### ✅ Viability Checklist

- [x] This wouldn't be a breaking change in existing TypeScript/JavaScript code
- [x] This wouldn't change the runtime behavior of existing JavaScript code
- [x] This could be implemented without emitting different JS based on the types of the expressions
- [x] This isn't a runtime feature (e.g. library functionality, non-ECMAScript syntax with JavaScript output, new syntax sugar for JS, etc.)
- [x] This isn't a request to add a new utility type: https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/No-New-Utility-Types
- [x] This feature would agree with the rest of our Design Goals: https://github.com/Microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/TypeScript-Design-Goals

### ⭐ Suggestion

By default, the [Jujutsu](https://github.com/jj-vcs/jj) VCS represents conflicts using a different style than Git. The overall conflict area is still delimited by `<<<<<<<` and `>>>>>>>` lines, but the intermediate sections are separated by `%`, `\`, and `+` characters instead of `=` and `|`.

Because this doesn't match `tsc`'s Git-based assumptions about conflicts, it generally causes the marker lines, the code they're enclosing, and nearby code to produce a lot of spurious errors, which is especially distracting when trying to clean up conflicted code in an editor.

The Jujutsu formats are documented [here](https://docs.jj-vcs.dev/latest/conflicts)—there's a default `diff` style where some sections are diffs with `+`/`-` lines and others are Git-style snapshots, and there's also a `snapshot` style where all sides of the conflict are represented by snapshots.

I took a stab at a basic version of this support in #64750, but there are some subtleties here that need more thought.

The two biggest issues are:
* The code for handling Git conflicts in TypeScript today works by parsing the first block of code (immediately following `<<<<<<<`) as normal, then consuming all non-marker content until the `>>>>>>>` marker. This is helpful because you still get type hints and whatnot for the first block, and you're less likely to run into errors in nearby code.

  In Jujutsu, there's always another marker line immediately following the `<<<<<<<` line, so a naive implementation would consume all code inside the conflict area. I think a reasonable equivalent to the Git behavior would be to process the first `+++++++` block, which marks a snapshot section, and ignore other blocks.

* If the actual text of a file contains any lines that look like a conflict marker, Jujutsu will use longer markers when representing conflicts. The scanner currently hardcodes the assumption that markers are always length 7. To be strictly correct here, we'd want to remember the length of the starting marker and then require the intermediate/ending markers to be the same length, so that we don't confuse the pseudo-marker that Jujutsu detected for a real one.

It seems to me that solving either of these problems would require the scanner to maintain state about the current conflicted area, which seems sketchy given how little state it's holding now. I'm not sure what solution would align best with the intended design of the scanner.

(There is an option that doesn't require scanner-level state, which would be for `scanConflictMarkerTrivia` to enforce a match between the length of the marker it's processing and the next one it's scanning to. This would require some ugly Jujutsu-specific logic for `<<<<<<<`, since we normally don't do any lookahead for the first marker, and it would still drop all of the code instead of preserving one block, but it would at least be better than the status quo.)

cc @jakebailey 

### 📃 Motivating Example

N/A

### 💻 Use Cases

Using Jujutsu to manage TypeScript code without having to either use the `git` conflict format or deal with spurious errors when fixing conflicts.

* If the actual text of a file contains any lines that look like a conflict marker, Jujutsu will use longer markers when representing conflicts. The scanner currently hardcodes the assumption that markers are always length 7. To be strictly correct here, we'd want to remember the length of the starting marker and then require the intermediate/ending markers to be the same length, so that we don't confuse the pseudo-marker that Jujutsu detected for a real one.

It seems to me that solving either of these problems would require the scanner to maintain state about the current conflicted area, which seems sketchy given how little state it's holding now. I'm not sure what solution would align best with the intended design of the scanner.

(There is an option that doesn't require scanner-level state, which would be for `scanConflictMarkerTrivia` to enforce a match between the length of the marker it's processing and the next one it's scanning to. This would require some ugly Jujutsu-specific logic for `<<<<<<<`, since we normally don't do any lookahead for the first marker, and it would still drop all of the code instead of preserving one block, but it would at least be better than the status quo.)

### 🔎 Search Terms

tsc --lsp, didOpen, project references, solution-style tsconfig, default configured project, "Deleting configured project", slow file open

### 🕗 Version & Regression Information

- I was unable to test this on prior versions because `tsc --lsp` is new in TypeScript 7. Tested with 7.0.2 on Windows 11 x64.

### ⏯ Playground Link

Not applicable: the behavior needs a project with several tsconfig files and an LSP client.

### 💻 Code

A solution-style `tsconfig.json` with two references:

```json
// tsconfig.json
{
  "files": [],
  "references": [{ "path": "./tsconfig.app.json" }, { "path": "./tsconfig.node.json" }]
}
```

`tsconfig.app.json` includes `src`; `tsconfig.node.json` includes the tool config files in the project root
(for example `vite.config.ts`).

### 🙁 Actual behavior

Start `tsc --lsp --stdio`, then open and close files under `src` one after another (`textDocument/didOpen`, `textDocument/didClose`).

Each `didOpen` searches both references. It finds the file in `tsconfig.app.json`, but still builds `tsconfig.node.json` and then deletes it again (server log, shortened):

```
Searching 2 project references of <project>/tsconfig.json
	Searching project reference <project>/tsconfig.app.json
		Creating ConfiguredProject: <project>/tsconfig.app.json
		Project contains file directly
	Searching project reference <project>/tsconfig.node.json
		Creating ConfiguredProject: <project>/tsconfig.node.json
		Program update for <project>/tsconfig.node.json completed in 18.5597ms
		Project does not contain file
Found default configured project for <project>/src/... : <project>/tsconfig.app.json (in 18.5597ms)
Deleting configured project: <project>/tsconfig.node.json
```

According to the server log, `textDocument/didOpen` takes 16 to 20 ms per file, while `textDocument/documentSymbol` takes about 0.5 ms.

### 🙂 Expected behavior

Once a referenced project directly contains the opened file, the other references are not built. Or a project built for the search is kept for the next lookup instead of being deleted right away.

### Additional information about the issue

I found this while adding `tsc --lsp` support to Serena, a tool that asks a language server for the symbols of one file at a time, opening and closing each file. In a project with 2643 TypeScript files, the repeated build of `tsconfig.node.json` adds about 50 s to a full pass. In a project with a single `tsconfig.json`, `didOpen` took 0 to 3 ms after the first file, which loads
the project.

### Comment

### 🔎 Search Terms

Keywords cannot contain escape characters, TS1260, escaped keyword, unicode escape in, instanceof, class field, ASI, automatic semicolon insertion

### 🕗 Version & Regression Information

- This is the behavior in every version I tried (5.9.3, 6.0.2, 7.0.2 and 7.1.0-dev.20261020.3), and I reviewed the FAQ for entries about escaped keywords and ASI

### ⏯ Playground Link

https://www.typescriptlang.org/play/?ts=Nightly#code/MYGwhgzhAEDC0G8BQ1pmgXmgRhdAOgK4IBsAnAL4B2qtd0A9A2tAGYCWApiACbRVgAtpz4ADdlVF4ARpmgAmPEVKUqEAC5gqwTgHtWqJiw7c+A4WIkatO-VIpIkwXWt0hOAOhC6A5gAoAeWkAK05gdQ8Aa04ATwg-Kk4Adzg-AEoMgG5GZgBtACIwfIAaaHyJErLpSvK1TW09VnyAXSQgA

### 💻 Code

```ts
class C {
  a = 1
  \u{69}n          // a field named `in`
  b = 2
  \u{69}nstanceof  // a field named `instanceof`
}

console.log(Object.keys(new C())); // ["a", "in", "b", "instanceof"]
```

### 🙁 Actual behavior

```
error TS1260: Keywords cannot contain escape characters.
error TS1005: ';' expected.
```

TypeScript treats `\u{69}n` as the `in` operator and parses `a = 1 in b = 2`. It does the same for `\u{69}nstanceof`. Then it reports the escape as an error.

### 🙂 Expected behavior

No errors. The class has four fields: `a`, `in`, `b` and `instanceof`.

A keyword can't be written with a Unicode escape ([5.1.5 Grammar Notation](https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-grammar-notation): "A code point in a terminal symbol cannot be expressed by a \ UnicodeEscapeSequence"). So `\u{69}n` is the IdentifierName `in`, not the `in` operator. It isn't allowed to continue the initializer, and it comes after a line break, so ASI ends the field there. `\u{69}n` is then the name of the next field, since a ClassElementName can be any IdentifierName.

V8 (Node.js) runs the code above as JavaScript and prints `["a", "in", "b", "instanceof"]`.

### Additional information about the issue

- TypeScript already accepts the escaped form when it doesn't follow an initializer. `class C { \u{69}n = 1 }` and `class C { \u{69}n() {} }` have no errors. Only the continue-the-binary-expression path after a field initializer gets it wrong.
- Without the escape, `in` on the next line does continue the initializer (`a = x` / `in` / `z` is `a = x in z`). That part is correct and covered by test262's `fields-asi-5.js`.
- Related but different: #54196 (escaped `constructor` reported as TS1260).
- Babel had the same bug and fixed it in [babel/babel#18365](https://github.com/babel/babel/pull/18365). That PR found this TypeScript bug through typescript-eslint, which fails to parse Babel's new fixture with "Keywords cannot contain escape characters".

### Disclaimer
Drafted with the help of LLM and I have reviewed this issue and verified that the content is correct.

- Without the escape, `in` on the next line does continue the initializer (`a = x` / `in` / `z` is `a = x in z`). That part is correct and covered by test262's `fields-asi-5.js`.
- Related but different: #54196 (escaped `constructor` reported as TS1260).
- Babel had the same bug and fixed it in [babel/babel#18365](https://github.com/babel/babel/pull/18365). That PR found this TypeScript bug through typescript-eslint, which fails to parse Babel's new fixture with "Keywords cannot contain escape characters".

### 🔎 Search Terms

import type default unresolved module, emitDecoratorMetadata design:type, TS1361 missing, getTargetOfImportClause, markSymbolOfAliasDeclarationIfTypeOnly, type-only alias not marked, ReferenceError `_1.default`




### 🕗 Version & Regression Information

- Reproduces from `typescript@7.0.2` to latest nightly.
- Does **not** reproduce in `typescript@6.0.3`, so this is a divergence introduced by the Go port.



### ⏯ Playground Link

https://tsgo.sxzz.dev/#

### 💻 Code

```ts
// tsc 6.0.3 reports (expected):
//   main.ts(18,11): error TS1361: 'Foo' cannot be used as a value because it was imported using 'import type'.
//   main.ts(19,11): error TS1361: 'Bar' cannot be used as a value because it was imported using 'import type'.
// typescript 7.0.2 / 7.1.0-dev.20261019.1 report TS1361 only for 'Bar', and emit
// `missing_default_1.default` for `Foo` although `missing_default_1` is never declared.
// (Both also report TS2307 for both imports; the modules intentionally do not exist.)

import type Foo from "./missing-default";
import { type Bar } from "./missing-named";

function dec(_target: unknown, _key: unknown) {}

class C {
  @dec a!: Foo; // tsgo: design:type references undeclared `missing_default_1`; tsc 6: Object
  @dec b!: Bar; // both: Object
}

const x = Foo; // tsc 6: TS1361. tsgo: no error, emits `missing_default_1.default`
const y = Bar; // both: TS1361
```

with options:

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "esnext",
    "module": "commonjs",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler",
    "strict": true,
    "esModuleInterop": true,
    "outDir": "dist",
    "declaration": false,
    "experimentalDecorators": true,
    "emitDecoratorMetadata": true
  }
}
```



### 🙁 Actual behavior

Both compilers report TS2307 for the two imports (expected: the modules do not exist). Beyond that, 7.x:

- Reports TS1361 only for `Bar`. No error for `const x = Foo;` even though `Foo` was imported with `import type`.
- Emits, for the `import type` default import:

  ```js
  __metadata("design:type", typeof (_a = typeof missing_default_1.default !== "undefined" && missing_default_1.default) === "function" ? _a : Object)
  ...
  const x = missing_default_1.default;
  ```

  `missing_default_1` is never declared because the `import type` declaration is (correctly) elided, so the module throws `ReferenceError: missing_default_1 is not defined` as soon as it is loaded. The `typeof` guard does not help because the reference is a property access on an undeclared identifier.

The named form (`import { type Bar }`) behaves correctly: TS1361 is reported and `design:type` is `Object`.

### 🙂 Expected behavior

Same as `tsc` 6.0.3:

```
main.ts(18,11): error TS1361: 'Foo' cannot be used as a value because it was imported using 'import type'.
main.ts(19,11): error TS1361: 'Bar' cannot be used as a value because it was imported using 'import type'.
```

and `__metadata("design:type", Object)` for both properties, with `const x = Foo;` left as a bare (unresolvable) identifier rather than rewritten to an import alias. This is the behavior `tests/cases/compiler/decoratorMetadataTypeOnlyImport.ts` already pins for the named-import form (type-only import of a type from an unresolved module → `Object`).


### Additional information about the issue

In `internal/checker/checker.go`, `getTargetOfImportClause` returns `nil` when `resolveExternalModuleName` fails without calling `markSymbolOfAliasDeclarationIfTypeOnly`, so the alias is never recorded as type-only. Every other `getTargetOf*` resolver marks unconditionally, which is why the named form works. (Strada avoids this via a lazy syntactic fallback in `getTypeOnlyAliasDeclaration` that was not ported.) The unmarked alias then makes `GetTypeReferenceSerializationKind` return `Unknown` instead of `ObjectType`, lets `GetReferencedImportDeclaration` substitute the elided import, and suppresses TS1361.

Adding `c.markSymbolOfAliasDeclarationIfTypeOnly(node, nil)` on the unresolved path, mirroring the sibling resolvers, fixes all three with no other baseline changes. Happy to send a PR

### 🔎 Search Terms

is a built-in extension and cannot be registered by a content mapper

### 🕗 Version & Regression Information

7.1-beta

### ⏯ Playground Link

_No response_

### 💻 Code

```json
{
    "compilerOptions": {
        "resolveJsonModule": true
    },
    "contentMappers": [{ "package": "json-const-content-mapper", "extensions": [".const.json"] }]
}
```


### 🙁 Actual behavior
```
> tsc --runExternalCode
error TS18066: Content mapper file extension '.const.json' is a built-in extension and cannot be registered by a content mapper.
```

this error message implies that `.const.json` specifically is a built-in extension, when in reality it's just `.json`.


### 🙂 Expected behavior

my preferred solution is that patterns like `.const.json` should be supported, to support content mappers [like `const-json-content-mapper`](https://github.com/jaydenfyi/json-const-content-mapper)

alternatively, the error message should be updated to clarify that `.const.json` isn't allowed because it conflicts with `.json`

### Additional information about the issue

relevant issue: #32063

body_text:
I've been unable to sign into my corp Azure account in VS Code. I've been able to replicate this in a transient VS Code session on a clean boot.

## Environment
- OS: Windows (Native Broker / WAM path active)
- VS Code: 1.108.1
- Auth runtime/extension: @azure/msal-node-extensions@1.5.25
- VS Code client id observed in logs: aebc6443-996d-45c2-90f0-388ff96faa56 
- Native Broker: enabled: true

## Steps to repro
- Install Azure Tools extension
- In Azure's Accounts & Tenants panel, click to add an account.
- Click Allow to allow the extension to sign in using Microsoft
- Select my Microsoft account from the account picker

## Expected behavior
Sign in succeeds

## Actual behavior
- The "Just a moment..." window flickers a couple times and sign in silently fails.
- MSAL broker reports missing/empty account id and realm normalization issues.
- Broker returns internal error `tag_7cisv `and `StatusInternal::Unexpected`, blocking normal auth flow.
- The JSON chunks in the logs mention a personal Microsoft account, which I've used in the past but not in this session.

When I restarted logs were unavailable. I looked for past session in $HOME/Library/Application Support/Code/logs but to no avail -- they were gone. Further, reviewed every file matched in: `fd -t f -p copilot -i -S +1b "$HOME/Library/Application Support/Code/logs"`, but unfortunately, all from the new session. Steps to Reproduce: 1. In `Plan` mode, in a multi-root workspace with (6 root folders across) two repos, I gave the agent a prompt that started with @workspace that involved reviewing many, many files 2. It came up w/ a plan that made it clear that it understood which repo it wanted to operate on (e.g., it included links to files in its output) 3. when I invoked `@cloud start implementation`, it took that whole context and invoked the cloud agent on the wrong repo from my workspace 4. Having no choice but to implement asynchronously, the cloud agent did it’s best to apply the same principles to a change in the other repo. 5. clicked restore context at the boundary right before `@cloud start implementation`, made sure I had no open files from the other repo, re-invoked. Same result, canceled the cloud agent again. 6. Removed the other folder from my workspace (now only 1 repo), clicked “restore context” right before the bad cloud agent invocation, then re-triggered. It went to the right place this time, but apparently it didn’t get any context. In the cloud agent, you can see it struggling: 7. Went back to my original chat which had gotten archived, and it now had no content other than this:

Type: Bug I have an organization-level custom agent defined in the .github-private repo. From reading the documentation, it sounds like that would be a _cloud_ agent, but I don't see that agent when I select "Cloud" as an agent type. In fact, I don't even see the ability to choose the name of an agent after selecting Cloud. I only see the ability to select a repository. This doesn't match the screenshots in the 1.109 release notes. It's confusing. With that said, I do see the agent defined in .github-private, but it's under Local. Why would it be a local agent? The VS Code documentation makes it sound like that would be a cloud agent. Is this a bug? Something wrong with my configuration? The docs should do a better job of clearly mapping the expected behavior. Overall, I find the VS Code documentation confusing in how it refers to custom agents. It doesn't explicitly state whether it's talking about a custom agent that a user can create from with VS Code agents dropdown or at the organization-level in the .github-private repo. For example, the 1.109 release notes do use the phrase "organization-level custom agents" in one place, but other places like the "Control how custom agents are invoked" section simply say "custom agent." Well, what type of agent are we talking about? Can I use the "user-invokable" setting with organizational-level custom agents, or is this only for the ones that you create from the VS Code agents dropdown? Every mention of "custom agent" could use a modifier to make this clear. Description

I often run multiple VS Code instances simultaneously, each with Copilot enabled (e.g., different repositories or experiments).

I would like:

A way to monitor and coordinate multiple VS Code instances from a single supervisory interface.

An optional scheduled or long-running autonomous mode (e.g., 24-hour cycles) to execute predefined workflows with proper safety controls and audit logs.

The goal is to enable coordinated, semi-autonomous development workflows across multiple projects, rather than isolated interactive sessions.

body_text: ## Feature Request VS Code [completion items](https://code.visualstudio.com/api/references/vscode-api#CompletionItem) can be configured to render their descriptions as markdown. Can you add markdown support for user snippets as well? I'd like to add links or markdown styles to make my notes cleaner. ```json "grid-auto-columns": { "body": [ "grid-template-columns: repeat(${1|auto-fit,auto-fill|}, minmax(min(${2:250px}, 100%), 1fr));" ], "prefix": "grid-auto-columns", "description": "Use `auto-fit` for expandable card or flexible images, use `auto-fill` for images or items of more consistant width" }, ``` ## Current Behavior CompletionItem vs User Snippet ## Ideas for implementation Some ideas to implement this: - Every snippet `description` can be updated to always render as markdown - Snippet descriptions only render as markdown if the user enables a setting - A new `markdownDescription` property is added similar to the one used in [json schema specification completion](https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/languages/json#_use-rich-formatting-in-hovers) I believe a new markdown description property would be the best approach.

Title: Copilot Chat sessions in a window with no folder/workspace open do not show local sessions from folder workspaces, despite docs saying the list shows all sessions across workspaces

Body:

## Summary

In a Remote SSH window, Copilot Chat sessions created in a window with no folder/workspace open (but with files opened directly in editors) and sessions created after opening a folder/workspace behave like separate local buckets.

In practice, the Sessions list does not show both sets of local sessions together.

This seems inconsistent with the current documentation, which says:

> The list of sessions is scoped to your workspace. If you don't have a workspace open, the list shows all sessions across your workspaces.

Docs reference:
https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/copilot/chat/chat-sessions#_sessions-list

## Repro Steps

1. Connect to a Linux machine using Remote SSH.
2. Start from a VS Code window with no folder or saved workspace open.
3. Open one or more files directly in editors from a Git repository, without opening the folder itself.
4. Create one or more Copilot Chat sessions in this no-folder/no-workspace context.
5. Confirm that these sessions appear in the Sessions list.
6. In the same VS Code window, open a folder or workspace that contains the same repository.
7. Observe that the sessions created in the no-folder/no-workspace context disappear from the Sessions list, except possibly for some cloud sessions.
8. Create a new local Copilot Chat session in the opened folder/workspace.
9. Return to a window with no folder/workspace open.
10. Observe that the local sessions created in the folder/workspace are not visible there either.

## Expected Result

When no workspace is open, the Sessions list should show local sessions across workspaces, as described in the documentation.

At minimum, local sessions created with no folder/workspace open and local sessions created in a folder/workspace should not appear to be mutually invisible if the UI claims that the no-workspace Sessions list shows all sessions across workspaces.

If this is intended behavior, then the documentation should clarify what kinds of sessions are excluded from the empty-window aggregation.

## Actual Result

Local sessions appear to be partitioned by context:

- a no-folder/no-workspace / untitled / anonymous workspace-like bucket
- a folder/workspace bucket

The Sessions list in the no-folder/no-workspace context does not reliably show local sessions created in the folder/workspace context, and vice versa.

Cloud sessions may still appear globally, which makes the behavior more confusing because some history is visible globally while local sessions are not.

## Why this looks like a bug

From a user perspective, this looks like an implementation mismatch between:

- the documented no-workspace behavior (show all sessions across workspaces)
- the actual session discovery behavior for local Copilot Chat sessions

It feels as if windows with no folder/workspace open are backed by their own anonymous workspace bucket, but that bucket is not actually merged with other local workspace buckets in the Sessions list.

## Environment

- VS Code: 1.116.0
- Copilot session metadata shows: copilotVersion 0.44.0
- Remote SSH session on Linux
- Reproduced when switching in the same window between an empty no-folder context with files opened directly in editors and an opened folder/workspace context
- Reproduced with local Copilot Chat sessions in the Chat view

## Local Evidence

On disk, local transcripts are persisted under separate `workspaceStorage/<id>/GitHub.copilot-chat/transcripts/*.jsonl` buckets.

In my repro, I can see separate local transcript buckets for different contexts, but the no-workspace Sessions list does not merge them as the docs suggest.

I also observed that:

- current local sessions are clearly written to `workspaceStorage/.../GitHub.copilot-chat/transcripts/...`
- I did not find direct evidence that these local sessions are later uploaded or merged through a simple cloud archive path on the remote host

So the visible behavior appears to come from session scoping/discovery, not from immediate transcript deletion.

## Additional Notes

This is particularly disruptive when trying to keep an active long-running chat visible while temporarily opening a folder/workspace in the same window. The session appears to disappear even though it still exists on disk.

This also affects a very common Remote SSH workflow:

- connect to a server over SSH
- work primarily from the terminal (`cd`, `ls`, build/test commands, etc.)
- open files directly in VS Code editors as needed
- avoid opening a folder in the Explorer because terminal-driven navigation is sufficient

That workflow is completely valid and works well for editing. In this mode, Copilot Chat is also useful and natural to start using immediately.

The problem is that once a folder/workspace is opened later in the same window, the previously active local sessions become invisible in the Sessions list. From a user perspective, this makes the chat experience feel fragile and context-dependent in a surprising way.

```
I found two useful things:

The server-side VS Code tunnel service is not installed right now. code tunnel status reports:

{"tunnel":null,"service_installed":false}
Also, your pasted error is almost certainly from the local VS Code desktop side, because it says Windows error code 5 (Access is denied). On Linux the permission code would normally be 13. So the quickest workaround is to start/install the tunnel from this server directly, bypassing the desktop singleton issue.

I started the official install command and it reached the auth picker successfully, then I stopped it so it wasn’t left hanging:

~/.vscode-server/code-560a9dba96f961efea7b1612916f89e5d5d4d679 tunnel service install --name qwen1 --accept-server-license-terms --log debug
It asked:

How would you like to log in to Visual Studio Code?
> Microsoft Account
  GitHub Account
Reply with Microsoft or GitHub and I’ll continue the install. After the browser/device-code login, I’ll verify code tunnel status and the user service logs.

9:28 PM
github
9:29 PM

15 previous messages
Done. The GitHub-authenticated tunnel service is installed and running.

Verified status:

{"tunnel":{"name":"qwen1","tunnel":"Connected","last_fail_reason":null},"service_installed":true}
The user service is active as code-tunnel.service, and I also enabled linger for trbot, so the tunnel should keep running after you disconnect from the server.

Useful commands:

~/.vscode-server/code-560a9dba96f961efea7b1612916f89e5d5d4d679 tunnel status
~/.vscode-server/code-560a9dba96f961efea7b1612916f89e5d5d4d679 tunnel service log
systemctl --user status code-tunnel.service
You should now be able to connect to the tunnel named qwen1 from VS Code / vscode.dev. Next useful thing: try connecting from your local VS Code Remote Tunnels view; if it still shows the Windows-side singleton error, restart the local VS Code app once, because the server tunnel itself is healthy now.

Asking Codex to fix was successful. It appears remote tunnel is trying to open the tunnel on the local machine, and not the VM I'm SSH'd to, and is failing to accomplish anything meaningful as a result. Codex output:

```
I found two useful things:

The server-side VS Code tunnel service is not installed right now. code tunnel status reports:

{"tunnel":null,"service_installed":false}
Also, your pasted error is almost certainly from the local VS Code desktop side, because it says Windows error code 5 (Access is denied). On Linux the permission code would normally be 13. So the quickest workaround is to start/install the tunnel from this server directly, bypassing the desktop singleton issue.

I started the official install command and it reached the auth picker successfully, then I stopped it so it wasn’t left hanging:

~/.vscode-server/code-560a9dba96f961efea7b1612916f89e5d5d4d679 tunnel service install --name qwen1 --accept-server-license-terms --log debug
It asked:

How would you like to log in to Visual Studio Code?
> Microsoft Account
  GitHub Account
Reply with Microsoft or GitHub and I’ll continue the install. After the browser/device-code login, I’ll verify code tunnel status and the user service logs.

9:28 PM
github
9:29 PM

15 previous messages
Done. The GitHub-authenticated tunnel service is installed and running.

Verified status:

{"tunnel":{"name":"qwen1","tunnel":"Connected","last_fail_reason":null},"service_installed":true}
The user service is active as code-tunnel.service, and I also enabled linger for trbot, so the tunnel should keep running after you disconnect from the server.

Useful commands:

~/.vscode-server/code-560a9dba96f961efea7b1612916f89e5d5d4d679 tunnel status
~/.vscode-server/code-560a9dba96f961efea7b1612916f89e5d5d4d679 tunnel service log
systemctl --user status code-tunnel.service
You should now be able to connect to the tunnel named qwen1 from VS Code / vscode.dev. Next useful thing: try connecting from your local VS Code Remote Tunnels view; if it still shows the Windows-side singleton error, restart the local VS Code app once, because the server tunnel itself is healthy now.
